articles.title: Rubio refuses to comment on Guilfoyle allegations
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday flatly refused to comment on a new report alleging that U. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle engaged in impr...
articles.body:
ATHENS, Greece (AP) — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday flatly refused to comment on a new report alleging that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before taking up her post.

Rubio told reporters that he would not discuss the allegations contained in a Wall Street Journal story that said Guilfoyle had asked a donor and supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.

He spoke before leaving Greece, where he delivered a speech calling for European countries to return to what he described as their civilizational roots.

Rubio said he was aware of The Wall Street Journal's report, which was published late Wednesday, but had no idea if it was true and he would not address it.

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," he said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart Greece, looked on.

At a joint news conference with the Greek foreign minister on Wednesday, Rubio said he would not address the allegations while visiting a foreign country, but added, "Suffice it to say our embassy here is doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."

The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees have called for an investigation into Guilfoyle, but Rubio would not say if he was prepared to open one.

Congressional Democrats already were looking into claims reported last month by the Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle acted improperly while serving as the top U.S. envoy to Greece.

The Journal reported that Guilfoyle told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.

Guilfoyle, a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump's son Donald Jr., has denied any wrongdoing and Rubio has defended her before.

This version corrects the day of the news conference to Wednesday.

articles.title: HUGH HEWITT: The midterms are one month out — you need to know the stakes
articles.summary: Chuck Schumer would block federal judges and Supreme Court nominees if Democrats win the Senate, using McConnell's own precedent against him.
articles.body: The short answer: If a "blue wave" materializes, the nation’s national security will be greatly compromised and almost no new federal judges or cabinet appointments of any kind will occur. The sort of defense spending the country definitely and urgently needs will not be appropriated, and if he becomes majority leader in the Senate, Chuck Schumer will shut down confirmations of almost all nominees from President Trump. What difference would those changes make? On the one hand — the hand that keeps a history textbook open — the answer is "not much." People expecting a "blue wave" may be disappointed that one or both of the houses of Congress don’t flip on election night, but even if they do, a different kind of disappointment awaits the left. LEE CARTER: POLLS SAY DEMOCRATS COULD SWAMP REPUBLICANS. AS A POLLSTER, I HAVE A QUESTION First, even the rosiest of scenarios for the left doesn’t give Democrats veto-proof majorities in both legislative chambers, the sort of one-party governance that, for example, has wrecked California. Divided government is a recipe for repeating government shutdowns, which can annoy and even destroy some things, but cannot bring about fundamental change. Democrats in D.C. cannot make all of America into California or New York without at least partisan control of all three branches of government and even then, the sort of change the Democratic Socialists of America demand — abolition of the Senate and packing the Supreme Court are two of their "must haves" — require at least supermajorities and probably Constitutional amendments. SOCIALISTS LAUNCH RADICAL PLATFORM TO ABOLISH THE US SENATE IN BID TO FUNDAMENTALLY TRANSFORM AMERICA The fever dreams of the left are thus going to remain unfulfilled for a very long time, because, no matter how often the "No Kings" canasta parties gather, the Constitution is very strong and doesn’t yield to fits of high revolutionary passion. It was built with the danger of precipitous legislative action in mind and, because deliberation is a feature, not a bug, of our constitutional order, it is rare indeed when anything happens fast. But significant damage would be done nonetheless, especially to national security spending. A lame duck Congress run by Republicans could try and pass a three-year defense appropriation, but if it can’t get that done between November 4, 2026, and January 3, 2027, the American military will be subject again to the sort of national security self-harm done during the years of "the Sequester." Democratic control of the Senate is also almost a guarantee that not a single federal appeals court or Supreme Court nominee would pass through a Chuck Schumer-managed Senate. Schumer would simply roll tape of then-Senate Majority Leader McConnell announcing "no hearings, no votes" in the aftermath of the untimely death of Justice Scalia. Schumer will argue that McConnell set the precedent. The optics of the different situations between McConnell’s refusal to move Merrick Garland forward in 2016 and those that result if a narrow Democratic Senate majority in 2027 blocks a vote on a Supreme Court nominee might be dramatic enough to wear down Democrats' resolve for revenge, but probably even a terrible look would not budge such a boycott and certainly not in 2028. Schumer would also likely refuse to allow votes on non-judicial Trump nominees no matter how far out the next election. His hold on the job of leader would be gone the instant he permitted a floor vote on any nominee of consequence, unless he was certain of the votes to defeat that nominee. MAJORITY LEADER THUNE WARNS CHUCK SCHUMER 'LIVES IN FEAR' OF SOCIALISTS TAKING OVER DEMOCRATIC PARTY We also know that the hard-left of the Democratic Senate nominees this year — Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, James Talarico in Texas, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, Sherrod Brown in Ohio, Chris Pappas in New Hampshire and Mary Peltola in Alaska — will be united with the anti-defense doves already in the Democratic caucus. What the country must have — a budgeted demand signal for the defense-industrial base — will flicker out. The rebirth of American shipbuilding will disappear too, even as China’s Communist Party cheers on the smothering blanket of big government regulation of AI/SI descending on its competitors in the United States. So a "blue wave" would do great damage, but there are some things such a wave could not do. President Trump’s continued command of the American military would be unimpaired, for example, nor would such a wave wipe out the re-mooring to the Constitution that has been ongoing at the Supreme Court for the past decade. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION So a blue wave would be very bad news, but it wouldn’t overturn the Republic. GOP candidates are on firm ground with warnings about the mess that would follow, giving majorities to Democrats but should avoid hysteria. Our adversaries abroad who are hoping for a Democratic wave should also remember that President George W. Bush ordered "the surge" after Republicans got "thumped" in 2006. If the rump regime in Iran is counting on Democrats to save it from Trump, they could not be more wrong. articles.title: America’s multibillion tech boom comes into focus as 7 key states put it to a midterm test
articles.summary: Voters across eight states will decide 34 data center ballot measures this November as America's AI boom becomes a growing political flashpoint.
articles.body: The rapid buildout of data centers powering America’s artificial intelligence (AI) boom is heading to the ballot box this November, as voters across the country weigh measures that could shape where and how the massive facilities are built. Voters will decide 34 data center-related ballot measures across seven states — California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Nevada, Ohio and Wisconsin. The measures come as states elsewhere have considered or imposed limits on development, underscoring how quickly data centers have become a political flashpoint. A Fox News national poll conducted last month found voters struggling to reconcile AI’s potential benefits with the economic and environmental costs of the data centers that power the technology. 8 EVERYDAY THINGS THAT WOULD QUIT WORKING WITHOUT DATA CENTERS More than seven in 10 voters (71%) opposed building AI data centers in their area, including 46% who strongly opposed them. More than half (52%) supported building them in remote locations, while 44% opposed. Overall, 60% of voters had a negative view of AI, compared with 37% who viewed it positively. That 23-point gap has more than doubled since a July Fox News poll. The Fox News poll also found a partisan divide over AI and data centers. Voters with favorable views of AI leaned Republican, while those with unfavorable views leaned Democratic. The divide was even sharper over data centers, with Republicans performing better among voters who supported them and Democrats among those who opposed them. That partisan split comes as AI policy emerges as a growing fault line in Washington and on the campaign trail. AI IS SUPERCHARGING POLITICAL AD WARS. BUT VIRAL DOESN’T MEAN VICTORIOUS President Donald Trump has opposed wide-ranging federal regulation of the AI industry and warned that the U.S. cannot allow China to win the technology race. But as the midterms approach, the debate over AI and the data centers powering it is playing out in races across the country. In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who previously courted major tech investments, recently ordered a pause on data center permitting and grid connections pending an audit. Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa has supported temporary moratoriums. ‘BACKWARDS AND POOR’: TRUMP SLAMS COMMUNITIES BLOCKING DATA CENTERS Meanwhile, in the state’s Senate race, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic state Rep. James Talarico have battled over tax breaks for the industry. In Ohio, the debate is playing out both on the campaign trail and at the ballot box. The state has 20 data center-related measures across 17 jurisdictions this November — more than any other state and more than half of the 34 measures going before voters nationwide. Trump, campaigning for Husted, defended the industry’s economic potential. "Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio, you can’t just turn them off," Trump said.

articles.title: Top conservative group unveils full-court press in key battleground state to expose ‘shocking’ Dem platform
articles.summary: Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America has knocked on over 172,000 doors in Iowa, saying voters are shocked by the Democratic Party's abortion stance.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX - CEDAR RAPIDS, IA : One of the largest pro-life organizations in the country is pouring time and resources into the high-stakes battleground of Iowa, making the case that voters of all backgrounds will be "shocked" to know where the Democratic Party stands on abortion. Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America’s ground game has knocked on over 172,000 doors in Iowa promoting the Republican ticket in the Hawkeye State. Additionally, the group has a planned digital spend of $650,000 to go along with a $1.35 million spend from the Women Speak Out PAC, SBA’s super PAC, to contact voters in the Iowa universe. "The scale of SBA Pro-Life America’s voter contact program is among the largest in the nation and certainly the largest in the pro-life movement," SBA President Marjorie Dannenfelser told Fox News Digital. Fox News Digital was on the ground in Iowa with SBA canvassers in Cedar Rapids on Tuesday, when the team passed out flyers and spoke to voters in support of Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson and hammered the abortion positions of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand. TRUMP-ENDORSED HINSON SECURES IOWA SENATE NOMINATION AS DEMOCRATS EYE GOP SEAT "Our goal really is just to inform voters," SBA field rep Amy Elizabeth told Fox News Digital. "Most people we're finding are pro-life, regardless of the way that they vote and we want to make sure that they're aware of the candidate's views on abortion and pro-life and we wanna make sure they're making knowledgeable and informed decisions when they go to the polls." Literature passed out by the canvassers calls Sand "wrong for Iowa families" while arguing that he will "do everything in his power to overturn Governor Kim Reynolds’ pro-life legacy" and "even supports painful late-term abortions." The literature also promotes Hinson as the "pro-life champion" that Iowans "need in D.C." Elizabeth told Fox News Digital that the conversations with voters on the ground have been effective. "Some of my favorite conversations have come from people who normally wouldn't vote the same way that I would vote," Elizabeth explained. "They're not typically conservative voters. They are a little bit more liberal-leaning. But when we really are open to having conversations together, and I can share with them some information about the candidates that they typically would vote for, they are very surprised, and they're very shocked to hear how those candidates feel on some issues that are important to them." NEW MIDTERM BATTLEGROUND TAKES SHAPE AS PARTIES BUILD ELECTION ARMIES Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America and Women Speak Out PAC announced in August that their Iowa voter-contact program had surpassed 100,000 visits to voters’ homes in the Des Moines, Davenport and Cedar Rapids areas. The groups said the effort is targeting persuadable and low-turnout voters ahead of November’s elections, with the goal of defeating Democrats they describe as "pro-abortion" and electing candidates who support abortion restrictions. Nationwide, Dannenfelser says SBA will ultimately reach 10.5 million voters during this election cycle, including 4 million at their front doors in person. "Our hardworking field team has been on the ground in key battleground states, educating voters about the Democrats’ radical agenda of all-trimester abortion — anytime, for any reason, paid for by taxpayers — even when babies can feel pain," Dannenfelser said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Polling shows the vast majority of Americans reject this, and our team at the doors is finding it true visit after visit. One conversation at a time, we are changing hearts, minds, and votes. We focus on Republicans, Democrats and Independents that can be persuaded and low-propensity, pro-life voters. All these groups are shocked by Democrats’ extremism on abortion." A third of Republicans would be less likely to vote in the midterms if they believe that the GOP has abandoned the abortion issue, according to polling released earlier this year, suggesting that driving pro-life Republicans to vote will play an important role in the party's hopes to retain control of Congress in November.

articles.title: Jordan emerges as potential next GOP leader if Dems seize House
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's top ally Jim Jordan emerges as a contender for House minority leader as GOP lawmakers brace for a full leadership shakeup.
articles.body: One of President Donald Trump’s most prominent allies in Congress could soon become his highest-ranking defender against a barrage of Democrat-led investigations and impeachment threats. Several House Republicans told Fox News Digital they expect the chamber will slide out of their control come November — and with it, a major shake-up in their top leadership ranks. "I don’t see a scenario where everyone gets to keep their job," one House GOP lawmaker bluntly told Fox News Digital. "I think [Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.] would be first out, and then [House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La.] has got to decide if he’s going to run for leader and, can he beat [House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio]?" Jordan and Scalise's names came up often, in Fox News Digital’s discussions with various House Republicans, all of whom spoke under the condition of anonymity to discuss internal conference matters. HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY A second House Republican said Jordan is the "number one name" in talks of a GOP minority leader. HOUSE CONSERVATIVES UNLEASH MULTIMILLION-DOLLAR MIDTERM BLITZ AGAINST DEM 'SOCIALIST' INSURGENCY The Ohio Republican already enjoys high name recognition among the party base. As the first lawmaker put it, "His celebrity status is very helpful … when Jim Jordan comes to town for you, you put 300 butts in seats." That status has been on full display so far this election cycle. Jordan has spent much of August and October traveling across the country campaigning for fellow House Republicans along the political spectrum, from vulnerable moderates to conservative MAGA acolytes. TOP REPUBLICAN UNLOADS ON RISE OF 'ANTI-AMERICAN' CANDIDATES HEADING INTO MIDTERMS: 'YOU GOT TO BE KIDDING' It’s a far cry from the Jordan who ran for speaker in October 2023, when former Speaker Kevin McCarthy’s ouster sparked a historic scramble to replace him. Jordan’s bid at the time was marked by fervent conservative support and fierce opposition from moderates, several of whom said they felt threatened by Jordan’s allies for their opposition. The first House Republican described his current persona as "Jim Jordan 2.0." "He's taken steps to, I think, build out way beyond the Freedom Caucus in terms of people that support him," that person said. "Like, he’s just a great citizen of the conference." But Jordan himself has not publicly pushed any leadership ambitions since the 2023 battle, when Johnson ended up speaker after several weeks of political chaos. The second House Republican said they’ve seen Jordan actively dismiss any such conversations. He told Punchbowl News earlier this week that he was "focused on winning" the House majority. The first person said, "I think [Jordan] quietly, without campaigning for it, has built up some infrastructure like that. But also, he could be throwing darts at leadership, and he's not. He's just trying to help us win." A third House Republican pointed out that, if Democrats win the House in another blue wave, many of Jordan’s most vocal opponents from 2023 will have lost their seats. And unlike a speaker race, where a majority of the full House is needed, a minority leader would only need to win a majority of the GOP conference. "If we lose 20 or 30 of those guys and all you’re left are guys like me, I think Jim Jordan's chances are much higher. Because the only people left in the conference are going to be conservative," the third GOP lawmaker said, adding they would "1,000%" back Jordan. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: FOR THE DEMOCRATS, WHERE COULD IT POSSIBLY GO WRONG? But a potential minority leader Jordan would not come without a fight. Most House Republicans are privately expecting Scalise, Johnson’s No. 2 and a member of House GOP leadership since 2014, to run for the job. "It’s very obvious they’re both jockeying for it," a fourth House Republican told Fox News Digital. "Jordan’s a pretty big draw for a lot of folks. I think he might have a play there. But there’s a lot of people who are loyal to Steve, especially those that have been around a while." Like other members of House GOP leadership, Scalise has also spent recess traveling the country campaigning for Republican candidates. He is also known as a prolific fundraiser for the party. A fifth GOP lawmaker said, "I would guess, at this point, that Scalise would be in the lead with Jordan running a close second." "And I think it would just depend on, you know, who would people see as a better fighter against the Democrats?" the fifth person posed. A sixth House Republican said a fight between the Louisiana Republican and Jordan seemed on the horizon if Republicans lost, and argued Scalise is best positioned to continue leading if that majority comes back. "In some respects, Jim Jordan, I think, would make a pretty good minority leader because he's a bulldog … [but] I've never believed that Jim Jordan would be an effective speaker," that sixth person said. "I think Steve Scalise probably is the best candidate that we have out there that has experience in dealing with the administration, that understands the must-pass portion of our agenda … and is our best negotiator." It would likely be a bruising battle, given there’s no love lost between the two men after their competing bids for speaker after McCarthy’s ouster. Scalise had won a majority of Republicans in a head-to-head against Jordan behind closed doors but ultimately did not see a House floor vote. Jordan's 2023 bid collapsed after he failed to clinch a majority on the House floor. JOHNSON DELIVERS BIG FOR TRUMP, BUT FRUSTRATION GROWS ACROSS RAZOR-THIN GOP MAJORITY But it’s not clear if it may even come to that. "I think that if Johnson runs for minority leader, he would still get the votes," the fifth person said. "He's done everything you could ask of a leader. He's raised the money, he's been on the road. He's cobbled together very difficult votes over the last two years that no one thought possible." There is also a world where Republicans defy expectations to keep the House. And in that world, Johnson is all but guaranteed to remain in charge. "Speaker Mike Johnson is an example of the American Dream. As Speaker, he's continued to defy the odds with a slim House majority and pass America First-bills," Trump’s campaign posted on X. "After Republicans win in November, they should re-elect Mike as Speaker quickly!" If the polls prove correct, however, most people are expecting Johnson to willingly step aside. "I don't think he's going to want to be minority leader after being the Speaker of the House, like, that doesn't make any sense to me," the fourth House Republican said. The third GOP lawmaker was more blunt: "Johnson’s done." Johnson himself dismissed any talk of leadership races in an interview with Fox News Digital last month. "I really haven't given it a moment's thought because we're laser focused," he said when asked if he would seek to be minority leader. "This is a midterm unlike any other, and I'm convinced we are going to defy history and keep and grow this majority." If Johnson’s prediction does not pan out, one member of leadership is expected to have a good shot at staying in his place: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn. Emmer has been privately telling House Republicans that he intends to run for the whip job again no matter what, multiple people told Fox News Digital, avoiding a possible collision course with Jordan and Scalise. "I think it was a brilliant move, saying, ‘You know what? I'm not going to do anything but try to keep my own spot,’" the first House GOP lawmaker said. "I think Tom's got pretty wide respect, and most of the hand-wringing from people was, ‘I don't want to have to pick between Tom and Jim.’" The fifth person said, "It's my understanding that Emmer is, if there is a race, going to be happy being the No. 2." But nothing is a sure thing in an environment where multiple House Republicans have said they are expecting a "bloodbath" in the midterms. Three GOP lawmakers told Fox News Digital they expect Democrats to win between 20 and 25 seats — with Republicans’ redistricting efforts sparing them from an even more devastating loss. A solid defeat, several House Republicans warned, could have people clamoring for a full leadership shake-up. The second House Republican said the entire leadership team could be "wiped out" in that situation. "It strikes me that there wouldn’t be a high likelihood of everybody just being OK with the status quo," the first person said. In that case, there is another name people see waiting in the wings for a potential leadership bid: Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas. "I keep hearing rumors but have not heard that directly," a seventh House Republican said. "My guess is that he is preparing to make a run in case the opportunity presents itself, but he’s being tactically quiet." The second House Republican said they heard his name second only to Jordan in terms of frequency. "When I was a candidate, I had no idea who he was, but he called me and gave money to my campaign," the first lawmaker said. "He’s very ambitious, but I don’t know what he’s aiming those ambitions towards." Several people speculated that he could run for the No. 2 job as whip if Emmer opted to step aside or was forced to. The fourth House Republican said they could see a world where Pfluger runs to be chairman of the House GOP campaign arm, the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC). "I think that he's positioned himself very well to be able to be in some sort of leadership position. I think it just depends on what that looks like," that person said. But there is one thing Republican lawmakers seem to largely agree on: November is not looking good. "Everyone that I have talked to across the country is seeing the same numbers that I'm seeing. So if you're in anything less than an R+6, I think you're at risk," the third House Republican said. articles.body:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D), is leading her Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman by double digits in the Empire State’s gubernatorial race, according to a new poll.

In the Emerson College Polling/PIX11 News poll, 52.4 percent of respondents said they would cast their ballot for Hochul, while 39.7 percent said the same of Blakeman. Nearly 8 percent of respondents were unsure on their vote.

Hochul’s nearly 13-point lead over Blakeman comes as Democrats face a favorable electoral environment heading into the November midterms. Republicans are being weighed down by issues including the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump’s sagging approval ratings and concerns about the cost of living as Election Day approaches.

Thirty-four percent of respondents said the economy is their biggest concern, followed by housing affordability and threats to democracy at 17 and 13 percent, respectively.

The poll also found Trump’s approval rating among respondents at 35.3 percent, with his disapproval rating at 57.3 percent. The percentage of respondents that were “neutral” or had “no opinion” about how they viewed Trump’s job performance was 7.3 percent.

Last December, Trump endorsed Blakeman for governor of New York.

“Bruce is MAGA all the way, and has been with me from the very beginning,” Trump, who is going to Syracuse, N.Y., for a midterm rally on Friday, wrote in a Truth Social post, touting Blakeman’s collaborations alongside border officials and police.

Hochul is the clear favorite to win November’s election in blue New York. Decision Desk HQ forecasts the incumbent has a 90 percent chance of winning the governor’s mansion for a second full term.

The Democratic governor won her 2022 election by about 6 points, defeating Republican Lee Zeldin, the current Environmental Protection Agency administrator.

The Emerson College/PIX11 poll took place from Oct. 3 to 5, featuring 900 likely New York voters and a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points.

articles.title: FBI post featuring El-Sayed runs afoul of Hatch Act, say experts
articles.summary: A new video from the FBI has spurred complaints the bureau has violated the Hatch Act by labeling Democrats – including current Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed – as part of the “defund the police crowd.” The video does not mention the election outright and also credits FBI Director Kash Patel with arresting violent criminals…
articles.body:
A new video from the FBI has spurred complaints the bureau has violated the Hatch Act by labeling Democrats – including current Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed – as part of the “defund the police crowd.”

The video does not mention the election outright and also credits FBI Director Kash Patel with arresting violent criminals and seizing fentanyl.

But experts say it clearly runs afoul of electioneering laws that prohibit federal employees from making such statements in a government capacity.

“Although the video does not direct viewers to vote for or against a candidate, its message that the candidates’ policies ‘failed’ and ‘Americans were left exposed’ is advocacy against their election that violates the Hatch Act,” Donald Sherman, president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington wrote on X.

“The video’s mention of El-Sayed as ‘Progressive Democrat, Senate Nominee’ clearly invokes the election. He is not a current gov’t official & his inclusion has no other purpose than to advocate for success or failure of a partisan candidate – a clear Hatch Act violation.”

The video, shared by the FBI’s rapid response account on X on Tuesday, is over two minutes long and features the faces of a number of prominent Democrats, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.) and Ilhan Omar (Minn.), as well as former Missouri Rep. Cori Bush.

“The DEFUND THE POLICE crowd wanted America to ‘reimagine safety.’ Translation: Let criminals run wild while cops take a backseat,” the FBI wrote in the tweet.

“They sold slogans. We delivered handcuffs. CRIMINALS FEAR RESULTS, NOT HASHTAGS.”

The video is backed by the beat to Michael Jackson’s “Smooth Criminal” and also features several clips of Patel on the job, including a scene of him walking away from a helicopter alongside Attorney General Todd Blanche.

“Talking about ‘defund the police’ isn’t necessarily what makes this ad problematic. However, when you start kind of bringing in the political party language and specific candidates for parties in political office, then the government messaging becomes problematic – a potential violation of the Hatch Act,” said Delaney Marsco, director of ethics at the Campaign Legal Center.

“If you are referencing political parties in a gratuitous way, in an inflammatory way, if it’s made close to an election, if it’s framed as an attack on a political party, that’s going to be political activity, and you need to be aware of how that’s going to run afoul of the Hatch Act,” she added.

“It shouldn’t shock anyone that this is not compliant with the Hatch Act.”

The video came shortly after Patel made an appearance on Fox News suggesting to the public how they should vote in the midterms.

“You may want to vote for people who back the blue, who fund law enforcement, who put terrorists and rapists and drug dealers in prison where they belong, and who manhunt people who wish to harm our way of life around the world, like this FBI does, thanks to President Trump,” he said late last month.

The FBI did not respond to request for comment for this story.

The FBI’s video has already generated a complaint from CREW.

“Although the video does not expressly mention the upcoming election or direct viewers to vote for or against a particular candidate, its message that the named candidates’ policies ‘failed’ and ‘Americans were left exposed’ reflects advocacy against their election and falls within the Hatch Act’s clear definition of prohibited political activity by covered members of the executive branch,” the group wrote in its filing to the Office of Special Counsel (OSC), which investigates Hatch Act violations.

“The video’s explicit identification of Mr. El-Sayed, one of several current candidates within it, as ‘Progressive Democrat, Senate Nominee’ is a clear invocation of the upcoming election. Mr. El-Sayed is not a current government office holder and is not engaged in policy-making with the FBI; certainly his inclusion appears to have no other purpose than to advocate for the success or failure of a political candidate.”

El-Sayed’s campaign did not respond to request for comment.

His campaign page does not comment on defunding the police but does advocate for abolishing ICE – U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

In a recent interview with Politico, El-Sayed said he did not feel that “defund the police” describes how he would approach policing issues, saying he would like to give local police departments more funding to recruit quality candidates.

“Look, it’s a pretty dumb and unnuanced slogan, which is why I understand Republicans really want to tie it to me now. But also, that was the conversation that was happening in every discussion I had about it. I took time to debate and define what I meant,” he said, including reform for cash bail, describing it as “discriminating against poverty” and having menta health professionals and other specialists on hand to respond to certain situations.

Beyond the FBI post, the White House has come under fire recently for other politicized messages broadcast using government resources.

That includes an ad campaign featuring Trump, showing images of the president overlaid with recent comments from speeches while featuring the song “Love Me.”

Trump and the White House were sued Wednesday by the Democratic National Committee for using Department of Homeland Security funds to pay for the ad, something they say violates various appropriations laws.

“The Trump Administration’s illegal use of taxpayer dollars for campaign-style advertisements deprives the DNC of a fair electoral process by adding public funds to the resources available to support Republican candidates,” the DNC wrote.

articles.title: Rogers, El-Sayed set to face off for first time in Michigan Senate debate
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed (D) and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) will face off in their first debate Thursday as they wrestle in the tightly contested race to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D). The debate will offer the candidates a chance to share their platforms and elevate criticism with one another’s political stances…
articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed (D) and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) will face off in their first debate Thursday as they wrestle in the tightly contested race to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D).

The debate will offer the candidates a chance to share their platforms and elevate criticism with one another’s political stances face-to-face less than a month out from Election Day.

The pair have traded barbs on the campaign trail, with the Republican accusing his opponent of being “ too extreme ” and the Democrat criticizing Rogers for his support of the Trump administration’s policies.

WOOD TV8, a Grand Rapids news station owned by The Hill’s parent company, Nexstar Media, will host the debate. The event will air live at 7 p.m. EDT, and each candidate will have a minute to respond to questions and 30 seconds for follow-ups, rebuttals and closing statements.

Rogers declined to participate in a debate against El-Sayed last month, accusing the host outlet and the moderator of favoring his opponent. The Democrat opted to take the stage alone.

El-Sayed has gained a slight lead over his Republican opponent in recent polling and won the support of the Democratic establishment despite early skepticism surrounding his campaign. The Democrat posted a 1-point lead in a Fox News poll and a 7-point lead in a Suffolk University survey last month.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned alongside the Democrat in Michigan a month after endorsing him . Later this month, on the first day of Michigan’s in-person early voting, former President Obama is set to stump for both El-Sayed and the state’s Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson.

President Trump has endorsed Rogers in this race, and the Michigan Republican has championed many of the administration’s policies on the campaign trail.

The GOP candidate notably broke with the president Wednesday when he called for an end to the trade fight between the U.S. and Canada after previously defending Trump’s tariffs as “necessary.”

El-Sayed has narrowly maintained a lead in Decision Desk HQ’s polling average since mid-August. The Cook Political Report , a nonpartisan election handicapper, rates the race as a “toss-up.”

articles.title: GOP efforts to lower gas prices derailed by Republican infighting
articles.summary: Republican efforts to reduce national gas prices in the weeks before Election Day were derailed in the Senate by infighting among GOP lawmakers and members of the administration who could not agree on how to ease consumers’ pain at the pump. The divisions within the Senate Republican conference over how to lower gas and diesel…
articles.body:
Republican efforts to reduce national gas prices in the weeks before Election Day were derailed in the Senate by infighting among GOP lawmakers and members of the administration who could not agree on how to ease consumers’ pain at the pump.

The divisions within the Senate Republican conference over how to lower gas and diesel prices — even if temporarily — were driven primarily by geographic differences.

Senators from oil-refining states shot down proposals from farm-state senators to ban the export of diesel or to loosen restrictions on the sale of E15 gasoline with higher ethanol content.

“You’re talking about regional politics, and it gets bogged down in the politics of energy, and the fiefdoms around it,” said Ron Bonjean, a GOP strategist and former Senate leadership aide.

There were divisions that went beyond geography, too.

Fiscal hawks torpedoed proposals to suspend the gas tax, even though their colleagues argued that doing so for a short period of time to bolster Republican candidates would have little real impact on the highway trust fund.

And lawmakers had less flexibility on some possible actions because of the depletion of the nation’s strategic petroleum reserve by big drawdowns to stabilize market prices during the Iran war.

The biggest problem, however, was that Republican senators didn’t see any proposal as likely to have a significant impact on prices before Nov. 3, when voters will decide which party controls Congress next year.

“It is almost impossible to federally reduce gasoline prices for consumers because the levers of power that can be used have very little effect on the prices,” Bonjean said.

The idea that appeared to have the most momentum was a proposal to impose a 90-day ban on diesel exports, which Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) began floating before a Senate Republican leadership meeting in mid-September.

“We need to concentrate on affordability for this election. With diesel at $6, the best thing [President] Trump could do is follow what a Republican president did in the ’70s and a Democrat president did in the ’70s — when they were worried about the price of food, they put an embargo on soybeans and wheat — and [Trump] should put an embargo on diesel leaving the country,” Grassley told The Hill on Sept. 14.

Trump embraced the idea, but it immediately ran into heavy resistance from oil-state senators and oil companies, who argued that it wouldn’t cut diesel prices but instead might even push them higher.

“One thing we know for sure is that export bans don’t have a negative price impact, particularly with a commodity like that that’s globally traded and globally priced,” said Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.).

“If you restrict access to the global market for our diesel production, you literally disincentivize more diesel production in which case you end up with higher prices, lower supply,” he said. “You’re restricting your global supply, which has a global impact on prices.”

Cramer warned that a diesel export ban “most likely would” raise diesel prices, especially in California and the Northeast, which import diesel from foreign sources.

Sen. John Cornyn (R), who represents oil-rich Texas, dismissed the proposed diesel export ban as a “gimmick.”

The White House in late September floated a plan to ban diesel exports for 90 days, despite objections from Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who argued that “banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work.”

Trump ruled out the idea last week before heading to Ohio to campaign for embattled Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio).

Earlier this year, fiscal hawks such as Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) spoke out against a proposal introduced by Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) to suspend the gas tax.

The federal gas tax is 18.4 cents a gallon for gasoline and 24.4 cents a gallon for diesel.

Hawley argued it would give American workers and families “immediate relief,” but Paul and other budget hawks warned it would blow a hole in the highway trust fund.

Another proposal floated by farm-state Republican senators alarmed by the voter backlash to high gas prices was to allow permanent easing of restrictions on E15 gasoline, a fuel blend that includes 15 percent ethanol.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), who’s up for reelection this year, touted E15 as a way to knock down fuel prices.

“It would bring it down right now, some people think, as much as 30 cents a gallon — do voluntary E15 nationwide. It would be immediately available. It’s there now. It’s an American product,” Rounds told The Hill.

“The president could do that today,” he said.

Rounds also called for expanding refining capacity in the United States. But Republicans from oil-producing states argued that wider availability of E15 gas would hurt small- and mid-size oil refiners.

Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) declared his opposition to what he called the “year-round E15 mandate” after Lee Zeldin, administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), announced in March that the Trump administration would expand the sales of gasoline with higher concentrations of ethanol over the summer.

The fight will continue to play out during the lame-duck session of Congress after the Nov. 3 elections.

Campaigning with Senate Republican candidate Michele Tafoya in Minnesota this week, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said he was optimistic about passing legislation to boost the availability of E15 gas in the stalled farm bill.

“I intend and expect fully to get this done and get it across the finish line,” Thune said of the farm bill. “And it will include E15, exact version maybe to be determined.”

Thune’s comments were reported by local radio station WZFG’s “The Flag.”

Even so, GOP strategists are doubtful that Washington can do much to impact the price of gas unless Trump finds a military or diplomatic solution to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has used to choke off much of the global oil supply.

“It’s very hard to predict where gas prices are going to be after the election but one could put money down it’s still going to be high,” said Bonjean, the GOP strategist.

He said, however, that prices could come down dramatically if Trump is able to eliminate Iranian threats to tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz using serious “military intervention” — something the president has alluded to in recent days.

articles.title: Democrats, with House majority, would go big on healthcare
articles.summary: House Democrats are promising immediate action on healthcare next year if they flip control of the chamber in the midterm elections. Party leaders say health costs are a foremost priority of their broader affordability agenda. And the top Democrats on the numerous committees that oversee federal healthcare programs are all preparing to tackle the issue…
articles.body:
House Democrats are promising immediate action on healthcare next year if they flip control of the chamber in the midterm elections.

Party leaders say health costs are a foremost priority of their broader affordability agenda. And the top Democrats on the numerous committees that oversee federal healthcare programs are all preparing to tackle the issue in the earliest phases of the next Congress.

“I see that as priority No. 1: Saving the healthcare of the American people,” said Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.), who’s in line to chair the Budget Committee if Democrats win the House majority.

The issue has resonated on the campaign trail all cycle, especially after President Trump and Republicans slashed health programs as part of last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, then allowed ObamaCare subsidies to expire in January. Polls indicate health costs are among the top issues — if not the top issue — on voters’ minds heading into the polls next month.

Democrats have seized on those anxieties, making healthcare a primary plank of their midterm pitch. Now, as the election odds continue to shift in their favor, those Democrats in line for gavels are already eyeing plans to pounce on the issue as a first order of business next year.

The push will feature legislation to reverse the Republican cuts and revive the Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies. But it also promises to extend much further than that, with efforts to expand paid medical leave and long-term care while challenging the controversial vaccine policies of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Even House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who has been exceedingly careful not to telegraph the specifics of the Democrats’ game plan for the majority, has made an exception on the healthcare front, telling reporters over the summer that it will be an early item on the agenda.

“We have made clear that we’re going to aggressively focus on making life more affordable, and I think we should begin in the areas where we know there is uniform Democratic support,” he said before the long recess. “We have to reverse the Medicaid cuts, [and] we should extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits.”

The Medicaid issue will be timely in January, since the bulk of the cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill don’t take effect until December, after the elections.

“That means that if we Democrats win the majority in November, and I get the gavel on Jan. 3, the Medicaid cuts will just be starting at the moment that I’m taking over as chair,” Boyle said. “I want to reverse every single healthcare cut that was contained in that bill.”

Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.) is poised to chair the powerful House Ways and Means Committee next year if the lower chamber changes hands. The panel has jurisdiction not only over a huge chunk of healthcare policy, including traditional Medicare, but also oversees federal tax policy. The combination puts Neal in a unique position to juxtapose those two issues, and he intends to use it to highlight the GOP’s decision, as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill, to cut low-income healthcare benefits to help offset tax cuts for corporations and well-heeled Americans.

“It becomes a different paradigm if all of a sudden, you’re being asked to cut healthcare so that you can offer tax cuts to wealthy people,” he said.

But Neal is hardly stopping there. He also expressed a strong interest in expanding federal funding for long-term healthcare services, which are getting more attention — and growing more important — as Americans live longer lives.

“There’s a complement to that, and it’s more dementia, more Alzheimer’s, more people are going to be needing [long-term care],” he said. “There is likely to have to be a government — a substantial government role in it.”

The Democrats’ healthcare wish list has little chance of becoming law, even if Democrats manage to win control of both chambers in November, because Trump will remain in power for the duration of the next Congress. But Democrats could use those issues as leverage in broader fights over government spending, as they did in forcing a 43-day shutdown last year over the ObamaCare subsidies.

Additionally, the debate surrounding those proposals is certain to become a part of the 2028 presidential race, which will kick off early next year, when the Democratic hopefuls are sure to make popular healthcare programs a major part of their platforms. In that sense, the House Democrats’ healthcare agenda will also serve as a form of campaign promise — and a glimpse at what the party might do if voters give them the House, Senate and White House in 2029.

The House Energy and Commerce Committee will be a major player in that conversation because of its outsized hand in healthcare policy and oversight, including jurisdiction over Medicaid, the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. (D-N.J.), who’s in line to lead the panel if the House flips, has been a persistent critic of the administration across each of those departments and subagencies. As a preview of his intentions, Pallone has bashed the GOP’s cuts to Medicare and Medicaid; hammered reductions in medical research as a threat to public safety; and challenged limits on mifepristone, an FDA-approved drug used in medication abortions.

Pallone has also raised alarms over the administration’s handling of a deadly measles outbreak in Pennsylvania, which could become a flash point in a presidential cycle where Josh Shapiro, the state’s Democratic governor, is expected to make a run.

Recent polls indicate that, for Democrats, healthcare is a winning issue. Family healthcare costs have risen steadily in recent decades, far outpacing inflation, and the trend is expected to get worse next year, when premiums are projected to jump again by double digits.

The factors behind the increases are varied, including the rising popularity of weight-loss drugs, consolidation within the industry and general inflation. But the expiration of ACA subsidies is among those factors, and voters appear to blame Republicans for the trend.

A survey released this week by KFF found that 60 percent of respondents are anxious about healthcare costs, and 42 percent of those people trust Democrats to address the problem, versus 22 percent who trust Republicans. (Twenty-eight percent trust neither party).

Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.), the ranking member of the House Education and Workforce Committee, which also has jurisdiction over certain pieces of healthcare policy, said Democrats won’t waste time responding to those voter concerns if the House changes hands in the new year. Among the priorities, he said he’ll be pushing to enhance family medical leave and restore the ACA tax credits.

“It’s a full agenda,” he said. “We have to undo what was done but then get back on the positive agenda.”

articles.title: Minnesota Senate hopeful warns threat level rising amid rash of Somali gang crime, terror plot
articles.summary: Republican Senate candidate Michele Tafoya warns of rising Somali gang violence and a foiled ISIS-inspired terror plot targeting Mall of America.
articles.body: The Republican Senate nominee in Minnesota is sounding the alarm about crime levels in the state amid a wave of Somali gang violence and a foiled terror plot by an American born to Somali parents. "I hear a lot of concerns from Minnesotans on the campaign trail about crime, and no matter what form that crime takes, Minnesotans know that they feel under a level of threat that has increased lately here in Minnesota, and in the last week and just today," Michele Tafoya, running as a Republican against Minnesota's Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, told Fox News Digital on Wednesday. "We saw the arrest of an 18-year-old Somali American citizen to Somali parents arrested for a terrorist — planning a terrorist attack — at the Mall of America during a Hmong celebration." The suspect in that alleged terror plot is 18-year-old Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, born in the United States to Somali nationals who are naturalized American citizens, law enforcement sources told Fox News Digital. Federal court documents said that Mohamud was arrested after purchasing an AK-47-style rifle, magazines and ammunition from an undercover FBI agent whom he believed to be a loyal ISIS member. MALL OF AMERICA TERROR PLOT THWARTED, SUSPECTED ISIS SYMPATHIZER ARRESTED, FBI ANNOUNCES The FBI alleges Mohamud had digital communications beginning in December 2024 with a confidential human source he believed was a member of al-Shabaab, a Somali Islamist terror group and offshoot of ISIS. "I can’t wait until I kill kuffar man. October 24 is the day insha Allah," one of the messages said. "Kuffar" is a term used to refer to non-Muslims, and "insha Allah" means "God willing." The Hmong people are indigenous to Southeast Asia and boast a relatively large population in the United States. "We have a large Hmong community here in Minnesota as well, and he basically stated that he wanted to take out anyone who was not a Muslim. He also noted that the Mall of America is owned by people who are Jewish," Tafoya said. "And so this was his plan, and thank goodness for the FBI in Minneapolis here and local law enforcement for catching onto this plan and derailing it well in advance. This is a guy who has pledged his allegiance to ISIS. Again, he is of Somalian descent and terror is alive and well and thank God we averted this massive crisis." TAFOYA MAKES 'COMMON SENSE' PITCH TO DISAFFECTED DEMOCRATS AS SHE VOWS TO FIGHT MINNESOTA’S ‘SOCIALIST LURCH’ The thwarted plot follows a rash of gang violence attributed to Somalis by law enforcement in the suburbs of Minneapolis. Police in Eden Prairie, Minnesota, said a shooting during the local high school's homecoming celebration last week was carried out by rival Somali gangs. Similarly, a shooting at a Bloomington, Minnesota, gas station over the weekend was attributed to Somali gangs. In the latter incident, more than 100 rounds of ammunition were fired. "And we have had Somali-related — Somali gang-related — attacks here locally in our suburbs at a high school football game during homecoming, at a Catholic Church parking lot, at a gas station, and this is all just really started to peak here in the last couple of weeks. So it's undeniable. Our law enforcement here are calling it out as the product of Somali gang violence, and we've got to identify it, and we have to find a way to deal with it." Tafoya also mentioned the Somali fraud scandals have enveloped Minnesota this year. BILL MAHER RIPS IMMIGRANTS WHO REFUSE TO ADAPT, SAYS AMERICAN VALUES ARE ‘NOT NEGOTIABLE’ "I don't know how you can legislate that assimilation, but we simply cannot tolerate the level of crime," she said. "We've seen it with fraud here. It's in the paperwork that the Feeding Our Future fraud was largely ... in terms of percentage, probably 98%, Somali people involved in that fraud," she said. "What I do think is any guests of this country who commits crime should be sent home with no pathway back," she said. "If you're coming here to be a guest of this country or to live in this country you cannot break our laws, and if you're an American, you cannot break our laws, period." Tafoya is not against immigration, noting that she's the granddaughter of immigrants, and she has an adoptive Colombian daughter who is as patriotic as they come. But she's not going to stop in her mission to battle crime, no matter the background of the criminals, she said. She plans to be an "equal opportunity pain in the a--" to all of them, specifically mentioning corrupt politicians. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I'm going to represent Minnesotans and Americans, and so there's, there's not going to be any limit on the way that I see crime. Crime is crime, and it's going to be committed by a wide variety of people, and they all need to be held accountable and accountability has been in short supply here in Minnesota. Fox News' Bill Melugin contributed to this report.

articles.title: Daylight saving time fight isn't over as House GOP presses Senate to end clock-turning forever
articles.summary: Trump shared Tom Cotton's cell phone number after the Arkansas senator opposed the Sunshine Protection Act for permanent daylight saving time.
articles.body: House GOP leadership is ratcheting up pressure on its Senate counterparts to pass legislation making daylight saving time permanent after President Donald Trump called on Congress to act. The House's No. 2 leader, Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., told Fox News Digital that "there's no reason Americans should lose an hour of sunlight at the end of the day when more daylight means more time with our families, more activity for our businesses and safer communities." "President Trump has been pushing to make daylight saving time permanent, and House Republicans delivered by overwhelmingly passing the Sunshine Protection Act. It's a commonsense change and the Senate should take it up," Scalise said. HOUSE PASSES DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME REFORM AS TRUMP SIGNALS SUPPORT FOR ENDING CLOCK CHANGE The debate over the twice-annual changing of clocks has raged for decades in Washington. Former President Richard Nixon's administration led the country through a temporary 16-month trial of year-round daylight saving, but mounting public frustration forced the experiment to end six months early. But the appetite for such a change appears to have returned. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act in a bipartisan 308 to 117 vote in July, and Trump posted on Truth Social Friday, "A ridiculous Clock changing process that takes place twice a year, costs our Country a fortune, is bad for Crime, stress on people, Sports, and just about everything else you can imagine." But the legislation is stalled in the Senate, where Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Politico there was "no clear path forward." TRUMP URGES SENATE TO PASS BILL MAKING DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME PERMANENT AFTER OVERWHELMING HOUSE VOTE It's created yet another rift between Trump and the Senate GOP majority, which he has clashed with on multiple fronts so far this term. Trump's frustration boiled over on the weekend when he targeted Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., one of the bill's most prominent critics. BATTLE OVER DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME ERUPTS AS PUSH TO STOP CHANGING CLOCKS HITS SENATE WALL "Almost everybody wants ‘The Sunshine Protection Act’ to pass, except for Tom Cotton," Trump said Saturday, sharing the senator's cell phone number. "To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate, and for America, itself." Cotton responded, noting that Congress has tackled daylight saving time before, only to roll back the change shortly after. SLEEP DOCTOR REVEALS THE BRUTAL HEALTH DOWNSIDE OF DAYLIGHT SAVING TIME "No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Saving Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," Cotton said on X. "Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first."It's a unique issue that has divided lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. There are others who agree with Cotton, who argue that sending kids to school in their states in the dark is a no-go for making the change. But there are also those who support the option and believe that Trump's added pressure could see the legislation resurface. But that will have to contend with an already stacked lame-duck schedule that will be heavily dictated by the outcome of the Nov. 3 election. "Look, obviously, Tom has very strong feelings, he's made those known both publicly and within the conference, so I don't expect that to change," Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., said. "You know, it's something, obviously, the people of Alabama, for the most part, have said that they're for." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "And so, we'll look for a pathway to have dialogue about it ... but I would anticipate, given the president's energy around it, that we'll have that dialogue and debate when we get back," she continued.

articles.title: Biden-era FBI records reveal sprawling Wiles monitoring as buried contacts surface
articles.summary: Declassified documents reveal the FBI tracked at least 39 contacts tied to Susie Wiles, monitoring her calls with attorneys and campaign officials.
articles.body: Newly released documents reveal the extent of the FBI’s monitoring of President Donald Trump’s now-chief of staff Susie Wiles, showing investigators tracked phone metadata reflecting her contacts with attorneys, journalists, campaign officials, Trump Organization personnel and Secret Service contacts. Documents released Monday by the White House detail "Plasmic Echo," the investigation into Trump’s handling of classified documents and other presidential records that led to the FBI’s 2022 search of Mar-a Lago and later included possible obstruction of the investigation. The records show the FBI tracked Wiles’ phone activity from at least February through May 2023, cataloging who called her, whom she called, when the calls occurred and how long they lasted. The documents show Wiles was in contact with at least 21 attorneys, along with campaign personnel, Trump Organization contacts, Secret Service contacts and journalists, offering a fuller account of the reach of the bureau’s monitoring. TODD BLANCHE EXPOSES HOW AGGRESSIVE BIDEN DOJ TARGETED LOW-LEVEL MAR-A-LAGO EMPLOYEES Reuters first reported in February that FBI Director Kash Patel said the bureau had subpoenaed phone records belonging to him and Wiles while they were private citizens as part of federal investigations involving Trump. The newly released documents provide a more detailed picture of the scope and scale of the monitoring, revealing how investigators mapped Wiles’ phone contacts across Trump’s legal, political, business, media and security circles over several months. Some entries name the contacts swept into the FBI’s monitoring of Wiles, including journalists associated with CNN, The Washington Post and Politico, while dozens of others are identified only by labels such as "Lawyer," "Campaign" and "USSS." Monday's document dump revealed the FBI’s monitoring also swept in Wiles’ contacts with two separate Secret Service officials, identified only as "USSS 1" and "USSS 2," extending the bureau’s mapping of her phone activity into Trump’s protective orbit. The records do not reveal what investigators were seeking to establish through those contacts, what was discussed or provide reliable durations for the calls. A March 24 entry from that year shows investigators logged a 41-second call from "Lawyer 7" to Wiles and then examined earlier calls between the two, illustrating how investigators were not simply capturing isolated contacts but tracing patterns across her network. The documents do not explain what prompted that scrutiny or what investigators believed those contacts could reveal. In another example, a March 9 log shows investigators cataloging a series of Wiles’ calls with at least six contacts identified as campaign personnel, recording when the communications occurred and how long they lasted, but not the substance of the conversations. JACK SMITH'S TRUMP PROBE SWEPT UP FOX NEWS, OTHER MEDIA COMMUNICATIONS AS INVESTIGATION WENT BEYOND LAWMAKERS The probe was launched by the FBI and Justice Department in March 2022, with then-FBI Director Christopher Wray seeking authorization and Attorney General Merrick Garland approving the full investigation. The probe was later placed under special counsel Jack Smith, whom Garland appointed in November 2022 to oversee the ongoing investigation. Wiles was running Trump’s political operation and serving as a top campaign adviser at the time, and later became his White House chief of staff. "Jack Smith’s surveillance operation was a disgraceful abuse of government power. Spying on political opponents is weaponization of law enforcement, plain and simple," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. "Those responsible must be held accountable." Heritage Foundation foreign policy expert Victoria Coates told Fox News Digital the tracking into Wiles is "unprecedented, dangerous and should be illegal." "The Biden FBI was following the precedent of the Obama FBI in 2015, when they used their authorities to surveil then-candidate Donald Trump and his campaign at Trump Tower as well as other candidates, notably my then-boss, Senator Ted Cruz. It’s the ultimate political dirty trick," said Coates. Coates argued that the breadth of the FBI’s tracking raises concerns about investigative overreach, pointing to what she characterized as a stark contrast with the Justice Department’s handling of President Joe Biden’s classified-documents case. "No, particularly by the Justice Department’s own very low standards in dealing with President Biden’s classified-document violations from his time as vice president, which were far more egregious than anything retained at Mar-a-Lago," Coates said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP She also warned that tracking Wiles’ communications with attorneys and journalists carries broader implications for future presidential campaigns. "In our increasingly digital world, it raises the grim specter of future campaigns where an incumbent can weaponize the private communications of not only a candidate and his family, but also his staff," Coates said. The declassified documents also show agents gathering details about the travel of Melania Trump and her son, Barron, as the FBI planned for a potential search of Mar-a-Lago. Operational planning emails included pre-raid checklists directing agents to "finalize FBI understanding of FPOTUS/FLOTUS/minor son's travel," including the type of aircraft and specific travel timeline, as investigators worked to determine when the warrant would be executed. The FBI executed the search warrant at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, on Aug. 8, 2022. Agents entered the property shortly before 9 a.m. and began searching around 10:30 a.m., according to records previously reported by Fox News Digital. Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price and Alec Schemmel contributed to this report.

articles.title: Lawsuit accuses Dearborn, Michigan, of being 'hostile to Christians and Jews' with Islamic displays
articles.summary: Margot Cleveland's lawsuit accuses Dearborn, Michigan, of displaying Ramadan banners and crescent moons while refusing equal Christian and Jewish symbols.
articles.body: Margot Cleveland, senior legal correspondent at The Federalist, is suing the city of Dearborn, Michigan, and the city’s mayor, Abdullah Hammoud, for violating the First Amendment by displaying exclusively Muslim symbols in public displays, accusing the city of being "a hostile place for Christians and Jews." Cleveland alleges the city put up banners celebrating the Islamic holiday of Ramadan and a display of crescent moons while refusing to showcase equivalent Christian or Jewish iconography. "I was picking up pizza in downtown Dearborn. When I went down the boulevard, up and down the street were ‘Ramadan Kareem’ (generous Ramadan) banners, which is the equivalent of a happy or blessed Ramadan," Cleveland told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. "This was the fourth week of Lent. We had Easter coming up in two weeks, and Passover was a week away. I was shocked, and then I saw the display all by itself — again, the crescent moon," she said. Cleveland wrote to Dearborn’s city attorney, asking if the city planned to reciprocate the displays for the other Abrahamic faiths, but did not get a response, she told Fox News Digital. SUPREME COURT SHOWDOWN LOOMS OVER ST MICHAEL STATUE BLOCKED FROM PUBLIC SAFETY BUILDING Cleveland submitted a series of Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests to find out the cost of the displays, which, according to her lawsuit and in an interview with Fox News Digital, is where she allegedly learned that the city had also integrated Islamic iconography in other official capacities. "The police department was selling — with the police department's seal — Ramadan T-shirts. It had the police department seal and a crescent moon, and I believe it said Ramadan," Cleveland said. CONNECTICUT BARS NATIVITY DISPLAY IN STATE CAPITOL BECAUSE IT'S 'RELIGIOUS,' LAWSUIT THREAT SAYS The Dearborn Police Department did not respond to a Fox News Digital inquiry regarding the alleged T-shirts. After repeated attempts to try and contact city officials, Cleveland still received no response, until one city councilor told her that the council had been instructed not to engage with her. TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS "I reached out to city council, every individual, both their public email and a secondary one. Received no response," she shared. "But on LinkedIn, one of the council members responded and said, ‘Hey, we were told we can't talk to you,’" Cleveland told Fox News Digital. Cleveland then attended an open city council meeting in May. She asked that the councilors, who she explained control the city’s purse strings, use an ongoing budget surplus to purchase banners celebrating Jewish and Christian holidays. GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS "I have not asked the city not to celebrate Ramadan," she said. "What I've asked is that the city treat Christians and Jews equally. Put up Passover banners, Easter banners, put up a Star of David, put up a cross, do something. And throw in some patriotic symbols to show we are one Dearborn, one country where all faiths are represented equally. That has not been done," she said. Contrary to acceding to her requests, Cleveland claims the city put up even more decorations celebrating Ramadan in the wake of her attempts to contact city officials. CALIFORNIA BILL RECOGNIZING 2 ISLAMIC HOLIDAYS NEARS NEWSOM’S DESK "After I was ignored, what happened? The mayor then went and bought more Ramadan displays. I complained about the banners. What does he go? He goes bigger and brighter with lighted Ramadan displays," she said. The mayor’s office did not respond to a Fox News request for comment. WORKING-CLASS AMERICANS SAY THEIR TOWN IS THE NEXT DEARBORN — AND THEY'VE HAD ENOUGH "People who are not in Dearborn do not understand Dearborn," Cleveland said. "My beef is with the mayor and the people running the city, who are discriminating against Christians and Jews. The average people who live in Dearborn get along great. It is a diverse city and people get along. The mayor is causing a problem." The city rejected Cleveland's accusations in a statement released shortly after Cleveland's lawsuit. Dearborn "has a longstanding commitment to serving all residents fairly and equitably, regardless of faith or background," the statement read. "Dearborn will continue to uphold the rights and dignity of every resident and remain a city where everyone is treated with fairness, respect, and equal protection under the law," the statement continued. The American Freedom Law Center filed the civil complaint on behalf of Cleveland in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan on Sept. 17. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Dearborn’s city attorney did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for additional comments. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: ‘No rules now’ — Putin’s war of open lawlessness is already targeting Europe
articles.summary: Putin’s new orders sound like total war — unrestricted in terms of the weapons used, the territory or combatants involved and the objectives pursued, in total disregard of the laws of war.
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of ordering his generals to abandon the rules of war and step up attacks on civilian targets and nuclear energy sites.

“He [Putin] said there are no rules now .”

That sounds a lot like the concept of total war — unrestricted in terms of the weapons used, the territory or combatants involved and the objectives pursued, in total disregard of the laws of war.

This is a complete disregard for the law of war — directly targeting civilians and facilities granted protected status. Putin’s “no rules now” is the very definition of a war crime. It is Russia saying, “I don’t care — just try to stop me.”

The U.S. and NATO need to determine when this becomes intolerable. Unfortunately, the answer appears to be only when it becomes inconvenient — like when it arrives on the doorsteps of a European capital.

No one wants to stand up directly to Russian aggression for fear of the response — except for Ukraine. Apparently, the law of armed conflict, the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and the additional protocols established in 1977 no longer apply in Russia, even though it is a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council with veto power.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is starting to get it. Last weekend during his visit to Kyiv, he called upon Putin to stop his “barbaric attacks” and end what he called a “senseless war.” That is something President Trump has yet to do.

Merz warned that “If Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us sooner or later.” He then pledged $1.5 billion in military and energy assistance and committed another $9.6 billion on defense cooperation, production, procurement and joint projects in Ukraine — namely, interceptor drones capable of countering Russian jet-powered drones and expanding production of long-range weapons systems.

For nearly five years, Moscow has been bombing residential neighborhoods , schools , hospitals , markets , churches , cultural centers , civilian transportation networks , and critical energy infrastructure . Russians have tortured and killed prisoners of war and civilians , created environmental disasters , attempted to cover-up atrocities in mass graves , and used white phosphorus munitions , chlorine gas , and more.

The Kremlin has been playing by “no rules” since day one. It is the Russian way of war and has been normalized by the West. The only difference now is that Putin is acknowledging his ‘no rules’ mandate. Apply Moscow’s actions in Ukraine to any other conflict in the world, and it would be called what it is — genocide.

Even so, only one warrant for the arrest of Putin has been issued by the International Criminal Court . It was for the “unlawful deportation of population (children) and that of unlawful transfer of population (children) from occupied areas of Ukraine to the Russian Federation.”

Yet Trump hosted the indicted war criminal in Anchorage, Alaska in August 2025 for a summit. He has now invited him to the G20 Leaders Summit in Miami this December. His purpose? To “ reintegrate Russia into the global economy” and “create a path for the U.S. to sign lucrative deals involving Russian oil, diesel, rare earth minerals, and other commodities.”

To acknowledge what Russia is doing would be inconvenient. It would require doing something about it.

Increasingly, Putin has convinced Trump that Ukraine is the impediment to ending the war. Not Russia, which started the war by invading, but Ukraine for resisting the invasion. Putin’s message: Peace can only be achieved when Ukraine submits to Moscow’s maximalist demands.

Trump has ignored the Kremlin’s war crimes and appears more focused on the potential of lucrative deals involving Russian oil, diesel, rare earth minerals, and other commodities with Russia than he is with holding Putin accountable.

Only now, Russia’s “no rules” campaign is extending beyond Ukraine to an active hybrid war campaign throughout Europe. The Kremlin has now turned its war machine against commercial shipping in the Black Sea region. On Monday, a Russian drone attacked and sank a Turkish-owned commercial vessel in Romania’s exclusive economic zone. The vessel was carrying grain and had departed Ukraine’s port of Izmail.

On Tuesday, Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev said that two commercial vessels were struck by sea and aerial drones — likely Russian — in an attack on shipping in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. One of the two vessels was carrying wheat from Ukraine. Radev stated that “What is happening is seriously disrupting shipping in the Black Sea, driving up insurance costs even further and making shipping extremely difficult.”

Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey are all NATO countries.

This is Russia, continuing to exert its will in a campaign of intimidation against European support to Ukraine.

Merz said that “if Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us.” Spoiler alert: It already has.

Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. They are the cofounders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.
