articles.title: House Republican warns CBDC 'communist money' could lead US to 'dystopian' future
articles.summary: Republican Rep. Warren Davidson of Ohio plans to introduce legislation that seeks to prevent the creation of a central bank digital currency.
articles.body: Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio, plans to introduce legislation that puts the prospect of a central bank digital currency (CBDC) in the crosshairs. The lawmaker, who has served in the U.S. House since mid-2016 and is currently seeking re-election, characterized central bank digital currency as "communist money for the digital age," during an interview with Fox News Digital. "They could just freeze your money. You could program it. Some people call it a feature," Davidson said. He provided a scenario in which a pickup truck driver pays $10 per gallon for fuel while a hybrid driver could get their fuel for just $2 per gallon. "And people see this as a feature. I think it's dystopian," Davidson said, adding, "I definitely want to stop it." Last month, in a post on X, Davidson wrote, "I'm drafting a bill to regulate Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) as counterfeit money. Planning a CBDC? Conspiracy. Designing a CBDC? Same as designing counterfeit plates. Launching CBDC? Counterfeiting. Prison for counterfeiters and their accomplices. No CBDC!" TRUMP TAKES UNUSUAL STEP, LETS BIPARTISAN HOUSING BILL BECOME LAW UNSIGNED AMID SAVE PRESSURE CAMPAIGN In another post on X last month, Davidson warned, "CBDC = communist money for the digital age. Programmable money puts the government between you and your money. You will only have access with their permission. This is an existential threat to western civilization." While a section within the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act that became law earlier this year temporarily prohibits the creation of a CBDC, that ban sunsets in a few years — language in the ban notes that "provisions of this section shall cease to be effective on December 31, 2030." Davidson told Fox News Digital during the interview on Tuesday that "the fundamentals for sound money is some level of fiscal discipline," adding that "you can't spend more than you bring in every year." "I don't think it has to be gold," he said, explaining that there needs to be "a disciplined monetary policy" in which "you can't grow the money supply disproportionate to your economy." HOUSE REPUBLICAN SUGGESTS SEN DARLINE GRAHAM IS AN 'ALLY' FOR THE 'SWAMP' "I think we should end this Fed," Davidson said, adding that he believes there is "a case for a central bank," while noting, "I don't know that you could reform the current one without ending it." Davidson said that he thinks "we should at least audit the Fed." Asked about President Donald Trump's proposal to dole out $5,000 to every American adult if the GOP wins both chambers of Congress during the midterms, Davidson indicated that he could get behind the policy if it is paired with spending cuts to cover the cost. GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US' CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Davidson said that "on its face" the proposal is concerning "because $5,000 per person going into the economy would fuel inflation," but suggested that such a move could be combined with action such as gutting Obamacare, saying that among "the most promising ways to pay for it is a radical shift in healthcare."

articles.title: Russia’s secrecy raises anxiety around plague
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ US presses Russia on plague ▪ Media outlets back in court ▪ DNC sues over Trump ads ▪ First Atlantic hurricane forming A lack of transparency from the Russian government about the status and severity of the suspected outbreak of the pneumonic plague is sparking worries around the world. The U.S. has…
articles.body:
A lack of transparency from the Russian government about the status and severity of the suspected outbreak of the pneumonic plague is sparking worries around the world.

The U.S. has sent a formal diplomatic complaint to Moscow demanding more information about the death of a lab worker at an anti-plague research facility in Siberia, a source familiar told NewsNation, The Hill’s partner network. The request came in the form of a demarche, an official diplomatic communication that can be used to protest or object to actions by a foreign government.

“We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information,” a State Department spokesperson said.

What’s known is that a 28-year-old female worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia died last week after being hospitalized with a severe case of pneumonia. Russian officials haven’t confirmed the origin of her illness.

Reports indicate that about 200 people in Siberia are under medical observation in the aftermath of the worker’s infection and death.

Unconfirmed reports have indicated the possibility of a second case in the outbreak.

World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a post on the social platform X on Tuesday that Russian health officials reported no cases of plague have been registered in the Irkutsk oblast.

He said they informed the agency that an epidemiological investigation has been conducted , preventative and control measures have been implemented, and identified contacts have been placed under medical observation and tested.

“They reported that no high-threat pathogens had been detected among the contacts and that medical observation of all identified contacts had been completed,” he said.

But this hasn’t satisfied the international community, particularly with memories of the COVID-19 pandemic still fresh in mind.

President Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that Russia said they “have it under control.” But he added that its information-sharing leaves more to be desired.

“Russia is sharing a little bit with our people. I want them to share a lot with our people,” he said.

Trump said Tuesday that he planned to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin about the situation “very soon.”

Secrecy is standard practice for the Kremlin, particularly as it has cracked down on free speech and other civil liberties under Putin.

Any outbreak appears to have been an accident as reports indicate the worker broke a test tube containing live bacteria, but Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) also raised concerns that Russia might be conducting biological weapons research involving the plague. He said additional scrutiny is warranted, especially given Russia’s history of a biological weapons program.

“We do know from defectors in the 1970s and ’80s that they were weaponizing the plague,” Paul told Fox News’s Will Cain in an interview. “So, this is concerning.”

The European Union is also on alert and is working to gather information about the situation.

European Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova told reporters that the EU has “channels” for getting information, Politico reported .

“We obviously would like to recall that timely and transparent reporting and access to reliable epidemiological and laboratory finding is essential,” she said.

The European Commission’s Health Security Committee, which evaluates serious cross-border health threats, held a meeting in Brussels on Wednesday morning, Euronews reported . The meeting had already been scheduled previously, but the Russia situation was added to the agenda.

Tedros said WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the pneumonia in the worker, the pathogen that prompted the measures and reports of a possible second case.

“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks,” he said.

▪ The Washington Post : How airlines could help, using lessons from the past.

Trump continued his back-and-forth with Canada on Wednesday, saying in an Oval Office event that “we don’t need Canada for anything.” I asked Rep. Pete Steuber (R-Minn.), who’s district borders Canada, if the president has it right.

“Canada is our best friend, a great ally, and the northern part of my district borders Canada. I’ve worked with members of parliament, talked about a lot of things that we have in common, and we’re talking about the USMCA, which is the best trade agreement with our three countries,” Steuber said. “I think we’re going to have a review of the USMCA and sharpen our pencils. I’m confident that our best friend and ally, Canada, will come to a resolution that works for both countries,” he added.

Minnesota, for example, receives a significant amount of natural gas from its northern neighbor. The standoff, especially heading into November , is an interesting conundrum for Republicans in those northern border states whose economies have tight ties to Canada.

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EDT/5 p.m. CDT on NewsNation.

Michigan Senate candidates Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed will face off for the first time tonight, in a debate hosted by Nexstar affiliate WOOD-TV. The Hill will provide coverage and analysis of the event, which runs from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. Nexstar also owns The Hill.

The majority of the Federal Reserve’s panel that sets interest rates believes another hike is likely to come this year, according to minutes released Wednesday from the committee’s last meeting. The committee will meet twice more before the end of the year, including toward the end of the month.

The Food and Drug Administration won’t publish its safety review of the abortion drug mifepristone until March, the agency revealed in a court filing Wednesday. It said it won’t impose any new restrictions on the pill before then.

BACK IN COURT: Lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico will appear in court today for a hearing on Trump’s efforts to revoke the credentialed press access to the White House for their journalists.

The three outlets won back temporary access after Trump moved in late September to bar their access, claiming their reporting endangered U.S. national security. However, the White House has continued to bar CNN and Politico from carrying out press pool duties on Air Force One.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly , a Trump appointee, is likely to extend his temporary injunction in favor of the outlets, as he previously ruled the White House must follow the decades of precedent in Washington that requires news outlets get notice and a chance to respond before their press access is revoked.

The media outlets are sure to raise the Air Force One issue as well.

Once Kelly issues his final decision, the Trump administration will be able to take the case to the court of appeals.

In a court filing late Friday, the administration’s lawyers argued the president moved to bar the media outlets because they “have failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.’”

The defendants responded in a court filing late Monday, saying the White House offered no new evidence to support those claims.

“At every turn since, Defendants have sought to justify the President’s ‘ban on the free press’ with a series of shifting rationales, lurching from unarticulated standards of professionalism to nebulous and pretextual concerns about protecting national security,” they wrote in the filing Monday.

▪ The Hill : Judge skeptical of FCC’s move to scrutinize ABC station licenses.

PIKE’S FIGHT: A Tennessee judge ordered the state to preserve all evidence related to Christa Pike ’s botched execution last week.

After a court appearance yesterday, one of the lawyers, Luke Ihnen , said he and his legal team have not yet asked the state to turn over evidence but instead wants it preserved “ so that her lawyers, experts, and the public can learn what really happened Wednesday night.”

“Today’s hearing was just a first step of many to preserve and enforce Christa’s constitutional rights after this unprecedented botched execution,” Ihnen said at a news conference.

Pike, 50, survived two lethal injections last week after she was scheduled to become the first woman executed by the state in more than 200 years. Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator for six days and woke up Tuesday and was speaking, according to her lawyers.

They said Pike has pneumonia and no function in her arms .

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) has halted executions in the state after ordering a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.”

▪ The Hill : Lawyers look to block Texas man’s execution after Pike incident.

NOT SO FAST : The Democratic National Committee (DNC) sued the Trump administration Wednesday over its taxpayer-funded ads, arguing they misuse congressional appropriations.

“The Trump Administration is using taxpayer dollars to air political advertisements, a blatant violation of the statutory ban on the use of appropriations for ‘publicity or propaganda purposes.’ President Trump personally directed this illegal activity,” the DNC said in its complaint.

Trump has faced backlash from both sides of the aisle over the ads, which denounce socialism and communism and tout his administration’s achievements. He said Monday he would pay for them through his own funds and from his super PAC instead of government money. However, White House officials have clarified he does not intend to reimburse the government for those already aired.

The DNC suit asks a judge to enjoin the government-funded ads, blocking them from airing.

THWARTED ATTACK: Federal law enforcement thwarted a terror attack by an 18-year-old Minnesota man who allegedly plotted to “commit a mass casualty attack on behalf of ISIS at the Mall of America,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said Wednesday.

The FBI had been investigating Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud for nearly two years. After months of exchanging text messages with a confidential informant for the FBI, Mohamud paid $600 for an AK-47 and 200 rounds of ammunition and was arrested on the spot, the FBI said.

The undercover FBI official was posing as a member of ISIS, according to court documents. In the text messages, Mohamud repeatedly told the informant that he intended to carry out an attack on non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24.

“This was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched,” U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said, praising the FBI agents, who “were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people.”

EXPANDING THREAT: The Hill’s Ellen Mitchell reports on rising concerns about Iran’s capabilities to attack far from its borders, following the security incident outside the U.S.-operated air base in the U.K. Sign up for Insider to check out reporting. The threat prompted the U.S. to move its 12 Air Force B-1 bombers stationed at RAF Fairford to home stations this month.

He has policy meetings and an intelligence briefing throughout the day before participating in a tele-rally at 6 p.m. EDT.

FBI agents stand outside the home of Lakiya Malone, who is charged with fraud involving federal homelessness aid programs, in Los Angeles, Sept. 16, 2026. (Jae C. Hong, Associated Press)

FBI GETS POLITICAL : The FBI’s video labeling Democrats, including Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed , as part of the “defund the police crowd” is raising complaints that the bureau has violated the Hatch Act.

The video doesn’t mention the election directly and credits FBI Director Kash Patel with arresting violent criminals and seizing fentanyl. But experts said that the video clearly violates federal laws that prohibit federal employees from making overtly political statements in a government capacity, The Hill’s Rebecca Beitsch reports .

“Although the video does not direct viewers to vote for or against a candidate, its message that the candidates’ policies ‘failed’ and ‘Americans were left exposed’ is advocacy against their election that violates the Hatch Act,” Donald Sherman , president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), wrote on X.

The video was shared by the FBI’s rapid response X account Tuesday. In addition to El-Sayed, it features former Vice President Kamala Harris , Democratic Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.) and Ilhan Omar (Minn.), and former Rep. Cori Bush (D-Mo.).

The video plays the beat of Michael Jackson ‘s “Smooth Criminal.”

“Talking about ‘defund the police’ isn’t necessarily what makes this ad problematic. However, when you start kind of bringing in the political party language and specific candidates for parties in political office, then the government messaging becomes problematic,” Delaney Marsco , director of ethics at the Campaign Legal Center, told Beitsch.

The FBI didn’t respond to Beitsch’s request for comment.

FIRST HURRICANE: Tropical Storm Isaias has strengthened to become the Atlantic season’s first hurricane ahead of its expected landfall this weekend on the northern Gulf Coast.

The storm is expected to make landfall as a Category 2 hurricane, with wind gusts of 100-120 mph, Friday night or early Saturday morning. Forecasters say it could peak as a Category 3 storm while over the central Gulf.

The latest forecast shows the storm on track to make landfall somewhere between the western Florida Panhandle and the Mississippi coast.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) on Tuesday declared a state of emergency for 25 counties. State agencies are preparing generators, flood barriers and other essentials in certain areas expected to be impacted.

This year has been a historically quiet Atlantic hurricane season amid the El Niño weather pattern. El Niño causes trade winds to weaken and pushes warm water toward the west coast.

This results in a more active tropical storm season in the Pacific and suppresses hurricane activity in the Atlantic. Warm and dry weather is common in the north, while cold and wet weather takes hold in the south.

This year’s El Niño is on track to be one of the strongest on record. This is the latest in the calendar that the first Atlantic hurricane has formed since 1914, a year in which no Atlantic hurricanes were produced.

The weather pattern may cause hurricane season to be quiet, but it can have wide-ranging implications around the world, leading to intense flooding in some areas and severe drought in others.

National forecasters expect El Niño to last for at least another six months and reach “super” strength in the fall or winter.

articles.title: Is AI a threat? Yes — it is already emptying Americans’ bank accounts.
articles.summary: The Consumer Federation of America puts 2025 losses to online scams and crimes at $148 billion — up nearly 26 percent in a year.
articles.body:
For the last few weeks, the debate on artificial intelligence and safeguards has focused on frightening questions — namely, could AI systems pose a threat to our human existence? The concerns are legitimate and have been shared by AI safety researchers and national security experts for years. But they have really gained attention after an Anthropic researcher warned about where the technology is headed upon his resignation.

These warnings of existential risks need to be taken seriously. But we need only check our text messages, social media feeds and online ads to realize that dangers from AI — namely, AI-powered frauds and scams — are already here.

While Congress debates what AI might someday do to humanity, Americans are already losing staggering amounts of money to online scams.

That is why, on Sept. 30, we joined more than 35 consumer protection, technology accountability, older adult advocacy and other civil society organizations to launch United to Stop Online Scams with a National Day of Action focused on AI and tech-enabled fraud. In partnership with the Motion Picture and Television Fund, we released a powerful PSA during a livestream featuring Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and Rep. Val Foushee (D-N.C.) that drew more than 50,000 views, while hundreds of people participated in events across the country.

We are calling on Americans to urge their state and federal lawmakers to hold online platforms accountable for their role in enabling the proliferation of online scams and fraud.

The Consumer Federation of America estimates that Americans lost $148 billion to online scams and crimes in 2025. That’s more than $1,100 for every U.S. household and nearly a 26 percent increase from the year prior. The same report underscores that AI-enabled fraud added over $6 billion in losses just last year. Older Americans are being hit particularly hard. Reported losses among people age 60 and older increased more than 59 percent in 2025, averaging $38,500 per reported incident, according to the FBI .

AI-enabled fraud has made scams remarkably easy that used to take significant time and effort to pull-off. Scammers once had to draft and send thousands of clumsy emails, one at a time, hoping at least one vulnerable person would take the bait. Today, AI can produce and automatically send messages, clone voices, generative realistic images, even tailor pitches to people’s vulnerabilities.

Criminals are using AI to create increasingly convincing scams with little effort, from deepfake videos of public figures promoting fake Medicare benefits to cloned voices impersonating loved ones in distress.

But scammers are only part of the problem. Some of the biggest tech corporations in the world operate the infrastructure that these scammers use to reach Americans, and they aren’t doing their part to keep us all safe. The Better Business Bureau’s latest scam risk tracker report found that social media was the contact method with the highest percentage of reports (more than 87 percent) involving monetary losses, with Facebook, Instagram and TikTok as the top reported platforms where scams originate.

Internal Meta documents showed the company anticipated roughly $16 billion of its 2024 advertising revenue came from scams or prohibited goods. Even more troubling, scam advertisers could be hit with dozens of violations before Meta permanently removed them.

AI-powered scams are a business-model problem as much as a technology problem. Our online ecosystem allows scammers to use AI tools to manufacture deception. Social media platforms help scammers deliver that deception directly to targeted audiences they seek to deceive. The corporations operating those social media platforms make a profit from scam advertisements that find their way to these victims. All the while, the burden for avoiding scams falls entirely on consumers.

Consumer education on how to spot and protect yourself from scams is an important part of the conversation. But too often, this discussion has ignored the responsibility Big Tech should have in preventing these harms in the first place.

Americans are being tasked with becoming experts in digital forensics just to navigate online spaces. But the corporations deploying these technologies and accepting payments from scam advertisers have far more resources to put protections in place that they simply are not pursuing.

AI and social media corporations must take reasonable steps to prevent their systems from being used for fraud or be held accountable if they do not. Social media corporations rely on revenue from advertisers, and should be expected to verify advertisers and detect and stop fraudulent ad campaigns. And when social media companies become aware that an advertiser is a scammer, the scammer should be immediately removed and banned from the platform — not just suspended or allowed to pop up under a different username.

The dangers of AI systems behaving unexpectedly and causing catastrophic harm deserves serious government attention. But there is also a danger in solely talking about AI consequences as if they are exclusively in the future. For millions of Americans, an AI harm crisis is already here.

Whether it sounds like a family member asking for money, a long-distance soulmate who wants a plane ticket to finally meet in-person, or a Facebook ad that is too good to be true, by the time the victims realize the person on the other side was never real, their money is already gone, and they are often too ashamed to ask for help.

JB Branch is director of federal AI governance and technology policy for Public Citizen’s Congress Watch Division . Richard Fiesta is executive director of the Alliance for Retired Americans .

articles.title: Trump interrupted by protesters at Texas rally: ‘They’re paid by enemies of our nation’
articles.summary: President Trump on Wednesday faced protesters who interrupted a rally for Texas GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton (R), with the president suggesting the hecklers were “paid by enemies of our nation.” In San Antonio, Trump was criticizing Paxton’s Democratic opponent James Talarico, when he paused amid an uproar in the crowd, The Associated Press reported.…
articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday faced protesters who interrupted a rally for Texas GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton (R), with the president suggesting the hecklers were “paid by enemies of our nation.”

In San Antonio, Trump was criticizing Paxton’s Democratic opponent James Talarico, when he paused amid an uproar in the crowd, The Associated Press reported . A man wearing a MAGA hat grabbed another man by the scalp and yanked him to the ground, prompting the president to say, “Let me ask you a question: Is there anything like a Trump rally?”

More protesters heckled, with at least one approaching the podium. Rally attendees pushed some of the demonstrators out, with Trump joining in to mock them. He at one point said the protesters “are really bad-looking people.”

“That guy’s got to lose a lot of weight,” he later quipped. “Many of these protesters are paid. You know that, right? They’re paid by enemies of our nation.”

At another point, the president asked that any “paid protesters” raise their hands and “get the hell out” of the rally, according to the AP .

He also doubled-down on controversial remarks he made at another rally earlier this week in Nebraska, where he suggested Iran could try to “take out” the Southern California cities of Los Angeles and San Diego. The White House defended the original remarks by arguing the cities are safe because the U.S. prevented Tehran from developing a nuclear weapon and calling out the media’s characterization of what he said.

“And I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way,” the president said Wednesday. “You want to see a horror show? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles. You want to see some bad things happen? You want to see a country in free fall? We’re not going to let that happen.”

California elected officials fired back at Trump in the days following the initial remarks, with Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) calling for the invocation of the 25th Amendment .

Golden State lawmakers in the House and Senate also demanded an apology . Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D), Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman (D) and San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria (D) all condemned the rhetoric.

Trump’s handling of the Iran war and rising prices have mired his approval rating. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday showed the president with a 32 percent approval rating, a record low that held steady from the polling center’s previous survey.

His loss of support has cast a dark shadow over the GOP’s prospects in the November midterm elections amid Trump’s request that voters pretend he is “ on the ballot .”

articles.title: Trump expanded mandatory immigration detention. Will the Supreme Court uphold it?
articles.summary: How can an immigrant in the country illegally be treated as an applicant for admission if he has already lived here for 20 years?
articles.body:
On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court granted the government’s request for a review of a Second Circuit Court decision holding that the mandatory detention provision in federal law does not apply to aliens who have been living illegally in the U.S. long-term .

The alien involved in this case is Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian citizen who entered the U.S. 20 years ago without being lawfully admitted and has lived here ever since. U.S. law provides that “if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained” pending removal proceedings .

But how can he be treated as an applicant for admission if he has been here for 20 years? The section of U.S. Code headlined “Aliens treated as applicants for admission” specifies that “An alien present in the United States who has not been admitted … shall be deemed for purposes of this chapter an applicant for admission.”

“ Admission ” is defined in federal law as “the lawful entry of the alien into the United States after inspection and authorization by an immigration officer.”

However, according to the Second Circuit, Barbosa da Cunha is not “an applicant for admission” because he is not actually “seeking admission.” Therefore, the court says, his detention is governed instead by another provision of U.S. law permitting discretionary release on bond or on conditional parole. And nothing in the language limits this privilege to previously admitted aliens.

The Second Circuit also relies on the fact that previous administrations have applied this section of federal law to aliens in Barbosa da Cunha’s situation for 30 years.

That may be true, but circumstances have changed. Those administrations did not have to deal with as many undocumented immigrants as the current Trump administration does, or with an immigration court backlog of more than 3 million cases.

The Second Circuit acknowledges that its view of these provisions has been rejected by some of the other circuit courts. But, it states, the “overwhelming majority of federal judges” have held that the government’s interpretation “defies their plain text.”

The government’s position was adopted in September 2025 by the Board of Immigration Appeals, “the highest administrative body for interpreting and applying immigration laws,” in Matter of Yajure Hurtado . Detention is intended in part to ensure that immigrants in removal proceedings will appear for their hearings. The practical importance of ensuring that they appear is illustrated by the fact that, as of July 24 of this year, about 279,000 of the 477,000 removal orders issued for fiscal 2026 were rendered in absentia — far more than 50 percent of all orders.

The provisions that the government is relying on were added to the Immigration and Nationality Act in 1996 by the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act. Before the latter was enacted, the law provided that all aliens arriving at a port of entry who were not “clearly and beyond a doubt entitled” to enter were subject to exclusion proceedings and mandatory detention, although the attorney general could grant parole. Aliens apprehended after making a successful illegal entry were subject to deportation proceedings. Aliens in deportation proceedings can apply for release from detention.

According to a February decision by the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act aimed to reduce this incongruity by also turning aliens who entered the country without inspection into applicants for admission.

Circuit Judge Steven Menashi wrote about this solution in his Sept. 25 dissent from the Second Circuit’s denial of rehearing en banc . He says, “It is true that unadmitted illegal aliens are not actually applying for admission,” as they are already in the U.S. But under the system that Congress enacted, those aliens are “deemed constructive applicants for admission.”

I expect the Supreme Court to reach the same conclusion Menashi reached. The law states that unadmitted aliens “shall be deemed for purposes of this chapter an applicant for admission.” And accepting that position would further what the Fifth Circuit has described as the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act’s objective: to eliminate the incongruity of giving aliens who achieve entry illegally a special opportunity to apply for release on bond that is not granted to aliens who lawfully seek admission at a port of entry.

Nolan Rappaport was detailed to the House Judiciary Committee as an executive branch immigration law expert for three years. He subsequently served as an immigration counsel for the Subcommittee on Immigration, Border Security and Claims for four years. Prior to working on the Judiciary Committee, he wrote decisions for the Board of Immigration Appeals for 20 years.

articles.title: On the Ballot: The state of the states: Which states are most likely to see trifectas in November
articles.summary: While much of the national focus this cycle has been centered on the competitive Senate and House races that will determine which parties control Congress, there’s plenty of reasons why folks should also be turning their attention to state Capitols and gubernatorial elections next month. State legislative races used to be sleepier affairs, but they’ve…
articles.body:
While much of the national focus this cycle has been centered on the competitive Senate and House races that will determine which parties control Congress, there’s plenty of reasons why folks should also be turning their attention to state Capitols and gubernatorial elections next month.

State legislative races used to be sleepier affairs, but they’ve grown in importance over the last 15 years, in particular, as both parties have started to invest more in the downballotelections. For one, local lawmakers pass laws that often impact constituents’ lives more directly and immediately than at the federal level.

Growing attention has also been placed on state Capitols and state Supreme Courts as local lawmakers and judges have been increasingly caught in the crosshairs on issues that have bubbled up at the national level – redistricting, abortion access, school choice and election disputes and law changes, among others.

State legislatures are also important to keep track of because they serve as incubators fordifferent issues and trends that can later catch attention at the national level.

Right now, Republicans hold more state trifectas (meaning a single party controls both legislative chambers and the governor’s mansion) – 23 – compared to Democrats’ 16. The remaining 11 states have divided government.

Trifectas give the parties tighter reigns on state power; the trifectas created after this November will give either party more authority to weigh in on upcoming consequential issues like data center and artificial intelligence (AI) regulations and open the door to more potential mid-dedicating redistricting.

Given the political environment this cycle, Democrats are projected to have a good cycle in state legislative chambers. But how good is another question.

“Even if we call this like a neutral environment, then I would still put Democrats as plus one because I would assume that Republicans would flip Kansas back because of the governor’s race, and I would assume that the Democrats would win Michigan and Minnesota trifectas,” Bill Kramer, vice president and counsel of state and local government relations firm MultiState, told On The Ballot.

Here’s a look at which states are most likely to see trifectas this fall:

If there’s one state that’s likely to become a trifecta this cycle, it’s the North Star State. Democrats already control the governor’s mansion and narrowly hold the state Senate.

Meanwhile, the state House is essentially tied between the two parties: Democrats hold 67 seats, Republicans hold 66 seats and there’s one vacancy that was left open by former GOP state Rep. Joe Schomacker.

After the 2024 elections, the Minnesota Democratic-Farmer-Labor (DFL) Party and Republicans settled on a power-sharing agreement that allowed Republican Lisa Demuth to become House Speaker while nearly every committee would have co-chairs from each party.

The DFL was buoyed earlier this year by the fact that it swapped out its gubernatorial nominee. Gov. Tim Walz (DFL) initially signaled he would run for another term but growing scrutiny around a statewide fraud scandal led him to backtrack. Recent polling suggests Sen. Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic nominee, will defeat Demuth, the GOP nominee, by between single and double digits.

“In Minnesota, the Democrats only need to net one seat [in] the state House to get it because the governor’s race [is] pretty much safe Democratic” with Klobuchar at the top of the ticket, explained Chaz Nuttycombe, executive director of State Navigate.

While Republicans have homed in on the statewide fraud scandal to put Democrats on defense, the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown – including two shootings in the state that involved U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) — threatens to stymiepotential gains.

State Navigate forecasts a 96 percent chance that the state sees a Democratic trifecta.

Kansas offers a rare bright spot for the GOP, who are likely to see a trifecta in the Sunflower State as the GOP holds both legislative chambers and Gov. Laura Kelly (D) is set to retire after this year.

Republicans hold comfortable majorities in each chamber: They hold a 31-9 edge in the state Senate and an 88-37 edge in the state House, according to Ballotpedia .

Kansas Sen. Cindy Holscher (D) is running against state Senate President Ty Masterson (R) to be the state’s next top executive, with recent polling showing the Republican up by 5 points, more or less.

Democrats face more headwinds here given Kansas went for Trump by 16 points in 2024, though the Sunflower State has shown more willingness to elect Democratic governors than Democratic senators in recent years.

While there is a competitive Senate race playing out between Sen. Roger Marshall (R) and Democrat Adam Hamilton, experts note that voters weigh statewide and federal races differently. Federal races are usually tied to the national party while gubernatorial races can see more split-ticketing because the race is inherently more personal to the voter.

But experts also note that the coalitions needed to win statewide versus downballotare different, too.

The voters that “matter to us may be … a slightly different version of Democrats than maybe sort of a tier one target of a different race,” explained Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee (DLCC).

State Navigate forecasts a nearly 80 percent chance that the GOP holds a trifecta in Kansas.

Democrats are also in a good position to gain a trifecta in the Great Lakes State where the state has a Democratic governor and the party holds the state Senate by a narrow 20-18 margin. Meanwhile, Republicans hold a 58-52 edge in the lower chamber.

Recent polling projects Democrat Jocelyn Benson will likely win the Michigan governor’s race next month against Republican John James, putting more of the focus on the legislative chambers. This state Capitol is particularly interesting given Trump won Michigan in 2024.

“Minnesota and Michigan are the the two clearest paths for Democrats right now because they literally had trifectas there a cycle ago,” explained Kramer.

While Kansas remains a likely bright spot for the GOP, Republicans have been clear-eyed that they face a tough election cycle in state Capitols.

“Our focus has been on making strategic investments that will give Republicans a chance to overcome historical headwinds and hold as many majorities as possible this fall,” Edith Jorge-Tuñón, president of the Republican State Leadership Committee (RSLC), told The Hill in a statement.

State Navigate forecasts a 77 percent chance that Michigan sees a Democratic trifecta.

What about Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and Arizona?

Three additional states to watch in November include the Badger State, the Keystone State and the Grand Canyon State for potential trifectas. All three states have Democratic governors, but only one, Pennsylvania, has divided control of the state legislature.

Wisconsin and Arizona, on the other hand, both have GOP-controlled state legislatures. So why are experts so interested in these three states?

In Wisconsin, a decision by the state Supreme Court’s liberal majority paved the way for new state legislative maps to drawnand made more competitive, giving Democrats an opportunity to compete more broadly across the state legislative map.

Democrats are bullish about flipping the state Senate, which has a GOP edge of 18-15, though they face a taller task in flipping the state Assembly, which has a 54-45 GOP tilt. Another unsure variable is the governor’s race between Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany.

Recent public polling has largely been minimal, though a Marquette Law School Poll conducted last month had Crowley up by a narrow 3 points.

State Navigate forecasts a 49 percent chance that the state sees a Democratic trifecta.

Arizona is another state that observers are closely watching. Gov. Katie Hobbs (D) is running for reelection against Republican Andy Biggs.

Republicans “have a very poor candidate there in the governor race, and … in 2022, another thing was just that the Democrats kind of underplayed their hands in the seats that they were playing in,” Nuttycombe said.

Adding in the fact that Latino voters look poised to swing back toward Democrats, it’s altogether “hurting Republicans’ odds of preventing a Democratic trifecta,” he added.

Kramer notes that Arizona has been Democrats’ figurative “Lucy and the football” as the party hastried multiple times to win one or both chambers and with no luck.

State Navigate forecasts a 73 percent chance that Arizona sees a blue trifecta.

A third state worth paying attention to here is Pennsylvania. Gov. Josh Shapiro (D), seen as a likely 2028 candidate, is all but expected to win reelection in November and Democrats hold a narrow 103-100 edge in the state House while Republicans maintain a 27-23 edge in the state Senate.

“The Republicans have a lot of strong state Senate incumbents in there,” Nuttycombe, said, who also added that “Pennsylvania is one of the biggest states for ticket-splitting in the country on the state level.”

State Navigate forecasts a 48 percent chance Pennsylvania sees a Democratic trifecta.

articles.title: Italian law to give election winners bonus seats: Why that’s controversial
articles.summary: Critics say the proposed law is undemocratic, potentially granting a winning coalition outsized power in parliament.
articles.body:
Italy’s parliament is voting on Thursday on a new electoral law that would make it easier for election winners to form a majority government.

The law, proposed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, would award extra seats to any party or coalition that obtains more than 42 percent of seats in both parliamentary chambers, ensuring it holds a majority.

Meloni has framed the legislation as a route to greater stability in Italy’s political system, which has often been run by fragile coalition governments. Her critics, however, say the move is actually aimed at boosting her own chances in elections next year.

Here’s what we know about the electoral law and what it means for Italian politics:

What is Italy’s current electoral system?

Italy currently has a mixed electoral system for its 600-seat parliament, with about 36 percent of members of parliament elected directly in constituencies where the candidate with the most votes wins, and the rest decided through proportional representation.

The system, called “Rosatellum”, has been in place since 2017. It encourages coalition-building but can produce fractured results that make a governing majority hard to forge.

The new legislation would replace the mixed electoral system with a fully proportional one, as well as awarding extra seats to the party or coalition that wins the most seats if it secures at least 42 percent in both chambers.

The bonus would be as many as 70 seats in the 400-member Chamber of Deputies, the lower house, and up to 35 seats in the Senate, which has 200 elected members.

That means if a party or coalition meets the 42 percent share threshold in both chambers, it would have stronger power to govern. If no party or coalition meets the threshold, representation would be decided proportionally.

The new law would also force coalitions to announce their candidates for prime minister before the elections. Rado Fonda, head of research at Italian pollster SWG, told the Reuters news agency this provision could “prove problematic for the centre-left, potentially forcing an early leadership contest and exposing divisions that could weaken the bloc”.

Meloni, who currently leads the country’s longest-serving government since World War II, has said the reform will help stabilise the country rather than serve any one political group. “Whoever wins the elections will have the numbers to govern,” she said.

The proposed law has already been approved by the Senate and must now undergo a final secret-ballot vote in the Chamber of Deputies.

Giovanni Orsina, a political scientist at Rome’s Luiss Guido Carli University, predicted that the law is “extremely likely” to pass.

If it fails, Meloni has said she will resign.

Opponents say the law is undemocratic because it could potentially grant a winning coalition a disproportionate level of power in parliament.

They also say that the legislation is intended to favour Meloni, whose Brothers of Italy party (Fdl) is bracing for a tough election battle next year.

Riccardo Magi, head of the liberal More Europe party, who is on a hunger strike to protest the proposed reform, has called it an “anti-democratic law” that risks giving a minority bloc a huge majority in parliament.

Senator Matteo Renzi, who leads the Italia Viva party, has accused Italy’s governing coalition of pushing the electoral reform due to a fear of losing power.

Other critics have pointed out that the law would do little to stabilise the political system if no party or coalition reaches the 42 percent threshold in both chambers – a relatively high bar.

“This could produce a hung parliament, making post-electoral negotiations necessary to form a government,” Vincenzo Emanuele, a political science professor at Luiss Guido Carli University in Rome and a member of the Italian Center for Electoral Studies (CISE), told Al Jazeera. “Even relatively small changes in coalition composition could make the difference between a clear parliamentary majority and a situation of political deadlock.”

When are Italy’s next elections, and what do the polls show?

Italy’s next general election must be held by December 22, 2027, although the government can call elections earlier if it wishes.

Currently, Meloni’s Fdl is polling ahead of all other parties, with 27 percent support, according to Politico’s polling aggregator. Her coalition partners, Lega and Forza Italia, have a combined 12 percent support, according to Politico, bringing the coalition share to 39 percent.

Fdl’s polling has been dented by support for a new far-right group, Futuro Nazionale (National Future), Reuters reported. It currently has 7.8 percent support, according to Italian polling institute SWG.

In opposition, the Democratic Party (PD) has 21 percent support, the Five Star Movement (M5S) has 12 percent and the Alliance of Greens and Left (AVS) has 6 percent, according to Politico. The Italy Viva (IV) and More Europe parties have 2 percent support each.

Emanuele said the current landscape means the proposed electoral law would not necessarily favour Meloni and could even benefit the opposition.

He said recent simulations by the CISE have shown that a centre-left coalition including the PD and M5S could potentially reach 44 percent of the vote, securing a “comfortable parliamentary majority”, though that could change if Meloni allies with National Future.

“The reform does not inherently favour the incumbent government: Its effects will depend crucially on how the competing coalitions are formed,” said Emanuele.

articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday accused Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D) of avoiding a debate with state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), asking, “Where is he?”

“Ladies and Gentlemen, upon information and belief, James TalaFREAKo, who is running for the United States Senate in Texas, is MISSING IN ACTION!” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “No one has seen him for an extended period of time.”

He continued, “Where is he? What is wrong with him? Bad rumors are coming out.”

The president added that Talarico should “immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able, one of the best Attorney Generals in the Country, and will soon be, hopefully, a United States Senator representing the Great People of Texas!”

Paxton’s campaign launched new ads this week criticizing Talarico’s recent absence on the campaign trail, with a voiceover saying the candidate had been “missing for 11 days.”

The Democrat last appeared at a fundraising event in New York with actor Robert De Niro on Sept. 28, but he revealed two days later that he was diagnosed with the flu during a virtual appearance at a U.S. Hispanic Business Council forum .

Despite Trump’s accusation, Talarico has accepted at least four debate invitations from CNN and local TV stations, the Texas Tribune reported . He challenged Paxton to a Fox News debate while speaking at the annual Texas Tribune Festival, saying Texans should “go to Ken Paxton’s safe space,” the Daily Texan wrote late last month.

“I’ll go into the lions’ den because I know what I believe,” he said. “I am proud of my record, and I’m not afraid of hard questions.”

The only debate scheduled for Texas candidates is for the race for railroad commissioner between Democrat Jon Rosenthal and Republican Bo French, a debate Rosenthal confirmed in late September. The forum has not been publicly confirmed by French, however, according to the Tribune.

The last Texas Senate race to go without a debate was in 2000 between former Rep. Kay Bailey Hutchison (R-Texas) and Democrat Gene Kelly, according to the outlet. The lack of any agreed-to debates in 2026 comes two weeks before early voting kicks off in the Lone Star State.

Paxton senior adviser Nick Maddux told the Tribune in July that “of course” Paxton would debate Talarico.

“Talarico is a serial liar who has spent his entire campaign shamelessly deceiving Texas voters about his radical record with[out] answering the hard questions,” Maddux said at the time.

articles.title: Congress can reclaim its spending and war powers by revising two policies
articles.summary: Lawmakers must learn from congressional history and reassert their authority to check executive abuse, particularly on the power of the purse and war-making.
articles.body:
In one of his latest examples of executive overreach, President Trump cancelled $810 million in congressionally authorized spending , yet again undermining Congress’s power of the purse.

From funding freezes to illegal wars, Trump has repeatedly tried to seize Congress’s constitutional powers throughout this term. The Government Accountability Office pushed back on the recent cancellation. And there are finally signs that Congress is starting to get fed up. Lawmakers from both parties are reportedly discussing how to adjust future spending bills to make sure this doesn’t happen again.

But Congress must go much further in clawing its power back. Lawmakers must learn from congressional history and reassert their authority to check executive abuse, particularly on the power of the purse and war-making.

The framers envisioned Congress as the foundation of the U.S. government, equipping it with the power to decide how taxpayer dollars are spent. While presidents and Congress have always engaged in a push and pull over funding, Trump is trying to burst through the remaining guardrails.

His approach harkens back to the 1970s, when President Richard Nixon refused to spend billions of dollars of approved congressional spending. In response, Congress passed the Impoundment Control Act , which reinforced its spending power by explicitly requiring the president, in most cases, to spend the funds Congress appropriates.

But presidents have manipulated vague parts of the law to justify funding freezes. In Trump’s second term, his administration has significantly escalated these tactics, gutting funding for independent agencies as well as delaying or withholding hundreds of billions of dollars of congressionally approved funds for foreign aid and more.

In many cases, courts have successfully intervened to force the administration to spend congressionally approved funding. However, Congress must enact proactive measures to ensure presidents abide by constitutional limits on power.

A first step could be for Congress to overhaul the Impoundment Control Act to remove ambiguities that this administration, and others, have used to justify withholding or delaying funding. Congress should also bolster its oversight abilities to make sure funds are being used and distributed appropriately. And in the aftermath of President Trump’s use of private donations to fund dubious projects like the White House ballroom, Congress must set stronger guardrails on when presidents can use private funding for projects, a process which allows them to bypass normal appropriations processes.

Another area where Congress must reclaim its constitutional prerogatives is war powers. The framers equipped Congress with exclusive powers to make laws and set national policy. The Constitution gives Congress, not the president, the power to raise, support and regulate the military and declare war.

At the tail end of the Vietnam War, Congress reaffirmed its authority over matters of war and peace by passing the War Powers Resolution , which recognizes that the president may use military force only when Congress has declared war, after Congress has passed an authorization for use of military force or when there is a “national emergency created by attack” against the United States. The law also requires the president to notify Congress of new hostilities within 48 hours and to terminate military operations if Congress has not authorized them within 60 days.

Despite Congress’s use of the War Powers Resolution to terminate the Trump administration’s illegal Iran War, the law has been an insufficient check on unauthorized conflict. Since the Vietnam War, presidents have overstepped the boundaries of their war authorities, Congress has struggled to rein in overly broad interpretations of presidential power and the courts have largely refrained from reviewing executive decisions concerning war powers.

President Trump alone has launched unlawful hostilities in Iran , Venezuela , Ecuador and elsewhere, all while stonewalling and even threatening congressional overseers. It took a full three-and-a-half months for Congress to take some steps to rein in the Iran War, and now months later the conflict roars on.

These challenges speak to the importance of Congress not only acting on Iran but also bolstering the War Powers Resolution to strengthen that law’s constraints. Experts agree on solutions including shortening the law’s 60-day window, clarifying key terms such as “hostilities” and adding a judicial review provision to ensure that courts are empowered to correct misinterpretations of the law and rein in abuse.

Half a century ago, when Congress passed the Impoundment Control Act and War Powers Resolution, it was doing so to stand up to a president who had stepped far outside the bounds of his authority. As Rep. Elizabeth Holtzman, who served in Congress during the 1970s, put it : “There were a lot of bills that became law which were in response to Nixon’s arrogation of power. Congress had finally said ‘enough is enough.’” Now, following decades of constitutional abdication and deference, the institution once again faces a president with seemingly no regard for separation of powers.

It is time for Congress to dust off and reclaim its constitutional authority — not only on this most recent canceled spending but on war powers and spending, generally — so it can be the people’s branch Americans deserve.

Maya Kornberg is a senior research fellow in the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice at NYU Law. She is also the author most recently of “Stuck: How Money, Media, and Violence Prevent Change in Congress.”

articles.title: Hecklers interrupt Trump Texas rally multiple times
articles.summary: President Donald Trump claimed protesters at his San Antonio rally were paid by enemies of the nation as he urged supporters to back Ken Paxton.
articles.body: President Donald Trump did not let multiple protesters step on his messaging in Texas on Wednesday night; in fact, he used the moments to claim that a Democrat-run city is using America's own freedom of speech to spread a left-wing agenda against his administration in the midterm elections. "You know, many of these protesters are paid — you know that, right?" Trump told the packed Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio. "Because you come in and, you know, they'll have like this perfect shirt on, made by the best printer money can buy." "I love where they all have the same exact size, beautiful pink and purple and blue and all different colors. And they're perfect, made by the same printer, very expensive signs," he added. TRUMP TOUTS ‘GOLDEN AGE’ AT OHIO RALLY, URGES VOTERS TO DELIVER GOP MIDTERM WINS "They don't make these signs. These are paid protesters," Trump claimed. "They're paid by enemies of our nation. No, I'm telling you, they pay them for this." Trump pivoted to his supporters who came out to rally with him for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, some waving cowboy hats. GOP FACES BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS REPUBLICANS PAINT ELECTION AS ‘COMPETITION WITH COMMUNISM’ As the crowd chanted "USA," drowning out several protesters who interrupted the event multiple times in a Texas city led by a Democrat, Trump added, "If there are any more paid protesters, please raise your hand and get the hell out of here." Trump is urging his base to turn out as if he is on the ballot in the midterms — because, as he says, the ability to pass his agenda in Congress is and his backers must help keep Congress in Republican hands. "We will not allow our country, our culture, our history and our heritage to be looted and plundered anymore," Trump said. "What they did to this country," Trump continued, pointing back to former President Joe Biden and his 2024 opponent Kamala Harris, "I said the other day, if Kamala won — or if that ideology won, forget about Kamala — if that ideology won, I don't believe we'd have a country anymore. I don't believe it. And now we have the hottest country anywhere in the world." REPUBLICAN CAVALRY ARRIVES FOR KEN PAXTON AS BIG-BUCKS TEXAS OFFENSIVE OPENS CASH FLOODGATES The battle for the Texas Senate seat between Paxton and Democrat James Talarico is one of the midterm battlegrounds that could determine Trump's fate in his final two years in office. "I will not let my legacy of having the highest vote in the history of Texas be tarnished or destroyed by allowing that travesty to happen again," he continued. "If they get in and do that and remember, like a guy like Talarico, it's basically one vote. It's so important — forget about for Texas, it's still just one vote — it's a killer in Congress because we have a very close majority. We can't let that happen. "If they get in, they will open your borders and let the entire world pour into our country like they did before. And we can't let that happen. We're not going to let it happen again." At least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president, including one who appeared to be close to the stage. Some were led away by police. Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption. TRUMP FIRES BACK AFTER PROTESTER INTERRUPTS MYRTLE BEACH RALLY FOR GRAHAM: 'MOM IS VOTING FOR US' "You know, I never talk about looks of a person, but those are really bad-looking people," Trump said about one protester. "You have to say they are bad-looking people. Come on." "No, he's going back to home to mom right now," Trump quipped. "What he doesn't know is that his mom voted for Trump." articles.title: We can build more without sacrificing America’s natural heritage
articles.summary: The Endangered Species Act must not be used as a bargaining chip in permitting reform negotiations.
articles.body:
America needs to build. We need affordable energy, a modern electric grid, more housing and infrastructure capable of meeting the demands of a growing economy.

But what kind of America are we building?

A prosperous country cannot be measured only in miles of transmission lines and pipelines, acres of data centers or megawatts of new energy. We also need abundant nature consisting of clean rivers, healthy forests and intact landscapes. A future dominated by concrete and steel but diminished of the extraordinary natural heritage that has defined this continent for eons is not abundance. It is a poorer America.

That is the false choice at the heart of the permitting debate now before Congress: that to build the infrastructure America needs, we must weaken the bedrock environmental laws protecting nature. Nowhere is that trade-off more misguided — or consequential — than in the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act .

For more than half a century, the Endangered Species Act has embodied a simple American value: Wildlife is part of our shared national inheritance, and we have a responsibility not to allow species to disappear forever.

Through the act — adopted with near unanimous, bipartisan support in 1973 — Congress gave that promise teeth through two key concepts: a prohibition on “take” of imperiled species and the requirement that federal agencies consult with federal government wildlife experts when projects they authorize, fund or carry out may affect those species.

In the last month, the administration has all but eliminated the “take” prohibition, including through a preposterous interpretation of the law that the destruction of habitat does not rise to the level of take. Common sense dictates that destroying the habitat an animal needs to feed, breed and survive can kill it just as surely as a bullet regardless of whether such harm was intended.

And now the permitting reform bill just released in the Senate will gut the consultation requirement by allowing that critical function to be delegated to individual states rather than federal agencies charged with the protection of wildlife for all Americans and not subject to the political winds and governmental priorities of any particular state.

Take. Harm. Consultation. These aren’t bureaucratic ornaments. They are the machinery that makes the Endangered Species Act work. Now that machinery is being taken apart, resulting in an Endangered Species Act in name only that is increasingly incapable of fulfilling its purpose.

And for what? The premise that consultation required by the act is preventing America from building is unsupported by the evidence.

A peer-reviewed analysis of 88,290 U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service consultations concluded that not one project was stopped or extensively altered because the agency found that it would jeopardize a species or adversely modify its critical habitat. Informal consultations typically took about two weeks; formal consultations about two months.

Consultation isn’t designed to stop development. It allows wildlife experts and project proponents to identify problems, reduce harm and find a way forward. The Endangered Species Act is not standing in the way of progress. It is how we make progress responsibly.

Clean energy or wildlife. Housing or habitat. Infrastructure or healthy ecosystems. These are false choices. A prosperous country that spans billions of acres should be capable of building what we need while protecting what we cannot replace.

That is what makes the current Senate political bargain so troubling and baffling.

The Trump administration has made gutting the Endangered Species Act a priority, and Republicans in the current Congress have proposed legislation to rewrite it only to be stymied by public outrage. Yet Democrats negotiating this permitting package have agreed to give them all they want, even with the prospect of them soon gaining control of both the House and Senate.

Why concede through negotiation changes that Endangered Species Act opponents have struggled to enact on their own, particularly when the evidence does not show that the law is responsible for America’s permitting problems?

Congress should tackle the barriers that actually prevent America from building. Improve agency coordination. Give wildlife agencies the staff and resources to make timely decisions. Address duplication and genuine bottlenecks. And perhaps most importantly, proactively identify low-conflict locations where transmission lines, energy projects and other large-scale infrastructure can be built quickly without resulting in unacceptable wildlife losses and damage to our cherished public lands.

But leave the Endangered Species Act out of it.

More than 50 years ago, Republicans and Democrats came together around the idea that preventing extinction is a national responsibility. They understood something worth remembering now: Wildlife isn’t an obstacle to America’s prosperity. It is part of what makes this country rich.

The Endangered Species Act must not be used as a bargaining chip in permitting reform negotiations. We can build the future America needs without sacrificing the natural heritage we share, need and love.

Andrew Bowman is president and CEO of Defenders of Wildlife.

articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday called Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) “terrible,” as the progressive battles former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) in a closely contested race in the Wolverine State.

“Mohammed El-Sayed is a terrible Candidate for the Dumocrats,” Trump wrote on Truth Social , using his nickname for Democrats. El-Sayed’s full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.

The president praised Rogers as “an extremely good” candidate, but said El-Sayed “goes back to days of the Jihad.”

Trump continued, “He is a RADICAL Extremist, Terrorist Sympathizer,” adding that the Democratic hopeful is “no different” from left-wing streamer Hasan Piker.

“Mohammed’s Values are not exactly those of Michiganders, or those of our Great United States of America! He is WRONG for Michigan, and WRONG for America,” the president wrote.

El-Sayed, who is Muslim, was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrants. He is the former director of the Wayne County Department of Health, Human and Veterans Services and defeated centrist Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) in the Democratic primary earlier this year.

Decision Desk HQ , a partner of The Hill, gave the progressive a 70 percent chance to defeat Rogers as of Wednesday. Nine days after the primary, the two candidates were neck-and-neck, with the Democrat holding a 51 percent chance of victory.

El-Sayed has campaigned on implementing Medicare for All, raising taxes on capital gains and billionaires and banning corporate PAC spending in politics.

He has also said the U.S. should cease funding the militaries of Egypt, Israel, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, blasting the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza as a “genocide.”

Rogers, who represented Michigan’s 8th Congressional District for 14 years, broke with Trump on his trade war with Canada on Wednesday. In a new ad , the Republican said the dispute should end “now,” after previously defending the levies on Canadian imports as “necessary” in a statement last month to USA Today .

The former GOP lawmaker did not mention Trump in his ad, and the president said Wednesday he thought the Senate candidate was directing his message toward Canadian officials.

“I viewed [Rogers] as saying that he thinks Canada should make a deal,” he told reporters in the Oval Office.

The president has repeatedly gone after El-Sayed since he won the primary, as Rogers looks to flip the seat held by retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.).

El-Sayed responded to the president’s attacks on Monday, saying Trump should “come to Michigan” and stump for Rogers.

“Your candidate can’t speak for himself. [Rogers] doesn’t have anything to say. Clearly, you are the answer, and you should tell everybody why they should imagine you on the ballot,” the Democrat told MS NOW’s “All In,” directing his remarks at the president.

articles.body:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s lawsuit against the Trump administration’s ban of the media outlets on White House grounds returns to D.C. federal court on Thursday morning. Despite a judge’s ruling two weeks ago that the outlets should be allowed in the complex for pool duties, the president has blocked them routinely.

Trump on Wednesday night doubled down on his comments suggesting Iran could hit Los Angeles and San Diego during a rally in San Antonio, adding that the U.S. would not let such a scenario play out. California leaders lashed out at the president after he suggested at a rally in Nebraska on Monday that the cities could be targets if Tehran developed a nuclear weapon.

On Thursday, the White House will hold a science summit. While is expected to unveil initiatives to strengthen America’s hand in evolving technologies, Trump is set to award trillionaire tech mogul Elon Musk with the National Medal of Science.

Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, has worked closely with Trump throughout his second administration. Last week, he was among several AI industry leaders to sign the new “morally binding” self-policing pledge . Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who was also among the signees, will receive a national honor during the summit, The Hill’s broadcasting partner, NewsNation, confirmed Wednesday evening. The event is slated to begin at 1:30 p.m. EDT.

Later Thursday, Georgia Senate candidates Mike Collins (R) and Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) will face off in a televised debate, scheduled for 7 p.m. EDT. As of Oct. 3, nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ has the Democratic incumbent nine points ahead of his challenger.

Nexstar’s WOOD-TV is also hosting a forum between Michigan Senate hopefuls Abdul El-Sayed (D) and former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.). Trump, who endorsed Rogers, blasted the progressive as “radical.”
